title: Preface
summary:
- SEC filing: Square, Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2020 (Commission File No. 001-37622).
- Company and securities details: Delaware corporation; principal office in San Francisco, CA; Class A common stock (ticker: SQ) listed on the NYSE; registrant phone number; IRS Employer Identification Number.
- Filer status and compliance: Well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; not a shell company; confirms timely filing of required reports and submission of Interactive Data Files; auditor attestation of internal control over financial reporting (SOX 404(b)).
- Market and share data: Approximate market value of non-affiliate equity as of June 30, 2020 ($38.7 billion); shares outstanding as of February 18, 2021 for Class A and Class B stock.
- Incorporation by reference: Portions of the Definitive Proxy Statement for the Annual Meeting incorporated into Part III.
- Table of contents overview: Parts I–IV covering Business; Risk Factors; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Market information; Selected Financial Data; MD&A; Market Risk; Financial Statements; Controls and Procedures; and other standard 10-K items.
- Forward-looking statements: Cautionary note outlining risks and uncertainties, including impacts of COVID-19, transaction and loan losses, PPP participation and liquidity effects, growth strategies and product development, expected benefits of products, GPV and revenue expectations (Seller and Cash App), product launches and acquisitions, IP, litigation, tax positions, share-based compensation, accounting guidance, restricted cash, and liquidity; no obligation to update.
- Business overview: Purpose of economic empowerment; evolution from enabling card acceptance (founded 2009) to offering 30+ products and services; effective June 30, 2020 reporting structure changed to two reportable segments—Seller and Cash App.
- Seller ecosystem: Integrated software, hardware, and financial services helping sellers start, run, and grow businesses; emphasis on cohesive, self-serve, digital tools and cross-sell; 2020 metrics include $103.7 billion GPV, over 2 billion card payments from 405 million cards, 210+ million buyer profiles, and ~295 million items listed.
- Cash App ecosystem: Suite of financial services aiming to make money management accessible—expanding from peer-to-peer payments to storing, sending, receiving, spending, and investing.

heading: Item 1. Business
start_phrase: We started Square in February 2009 to enable businesses (sellers) to accept card payments, an important capability that was previously inaccessible tomany businesses.
summary:
- Company overview and segmentation: Origins of Square (2009), purpose of economic empowerment, expansion to two reportable segments as of June 30, 2020—Seller and Cash App—reflecting distinct ecosystems and management reporting.
- Seller ecosystem: Cohesive suite of 30+ software, hardware, and financial services enabling sellers to start, run, and grow businesses; emphasis on integrated, self-serve, omnichannel tools and efficient cross-sell. 2020 metrics: $103.7B GPV from 2B+ card payments and 405M cards; 210M buyer profiles; ~295M items listed; rising mix of larger sellers (60% of Q4 2020 GPV).
- Seller software: POS (Square Point of Sale, Appointments, Retail, Restaurants), online commerce (Square Online, Online Checkout, Invoices, Virtual Terminal), CRM and operations (Team Management, Contracts, Loyalty, Marketing, Gift Cards, Feedback, Dashboard); monetization via transaction, subscription, and service fees; developer platform with Payment and Commerce APIs/SDKs.
- Seller hardware: Magstripe reader, Contactless and Chip reader, Square Stand, Register, and Terminal; compatibility with major card networks and accessories.
- Seller financial services: Managed Payments (settlement, disputes, PCI), Risk Manager, Instant Transfer, Square Card (prepaid debit; interchange revenue), Square Capital (data-driven loan facilitation including PPP; forward-flow funding), Square Payroll; plan to launch Square Financial Services (ILC) in 2021, pending regulatory approval.
- Cash App ecosystem: Consumer financial services enabling storing, sending, receiving, spending, and investing; strong brand and simple UX; serves primarily the U.S., with some European services.
- Cash App products: P2P transfers, stored balances (approx. $2.0B as of 12/31/2020), direct deposit (routing/account numbers), cross-border U.S.–U.K. payments; Cash Card debit with Boost rewards (interchange revenue); investing in stocks/ETFs (including fractional) and bitcoin (revenue recognized on customer bitcoin purchases); addition of tax filing via acquisition of Credit Karma Tax.
- Cash App scale and engagement: 36M+ monthly transacting actives as of Dec 2020; top-ranked finance app by U.S. downloads in 2020.
- COVID-19 response: Fee waivers and subscription pauses for sellers; acceleration of omnichannel features (online, curbside, delivery, eGift Cards); free marketing campaigns; facilitation of ~$857M PPP loans to 80k+ small businesses. For Cash App: education on CARES Act, expanded direct deposit for government funds, Boost adaptations to pandemic-relevant categories.
- Customers and markets: Diverse seller base by industry, size, and geography (U.S., Canada, Japan, Australia, U.K.); no single customer >5% of GPV or revenue in 2018–2020. Cash App customers across all 50 states and nearly every U.S. county; presence in Europe.
- Sales and marketing: Strong brands; Seller NPS ~65; acquisition via direct marketing, PR, direct sales for larger sellers, and >700 partners via App Marketplace; scalable in-product communication. Cash App growth led by P2P network effects, referrals, paid advertising, partnerships, and feature launches.
- Product development and technology: Cross-platform, rapid release cadence, scalable infrastructure, heavy use of data science/ML (automated risk >99.95% of transactions); in-house hardware design with third-party manufacturing.
- Competition: Seller ecosystem competes with manual processes, business software vendors, payment terminal providers, merchant acquirers, banks, payroll processors, and alternative lenders; differentiation via integrated ecosystem, UX, transparent pricing, and innovation. Cash App competes with P2P apps, debit/prepaid offerings, rewards programs, brokerages, and crypto services; competes on brand and simplicity.
- Human capital: 5,477 full-time employees (662 outside U.S.) as of Dec 31, 2020; purpose-driven culture, remote-work flexibility, learning and manager training, inclusion and diversity focus (public reporting), competitive total rewards and annual pay equity analyses.
- Intellectual property: Protection via contracts, trademarks, copyrights, domains, trade secrets, and patents; ongoing patent program; use of some licensed/open-source technology.
- Government and regulatory environment: Extensive U.S. and international compliance across payments licensing (money transmission, MSB registration), consumer protection, AML, bank regulation (FDIC/Utah approvals for ILC), broker-dealer rules for Cash App Investing (SEC/FINRA/state), virtual currency (NY BitLicense) and potential additional licensing; privacy/data protection; communications laws; other evolving regulatory areas.
- Seasonality and revenue mix: Seller transaction revenue typically strongest in Q4; Cash App seasonality tied to government funds and tax refunds; 2020 results skewed by significant bitcoin revenue (48% of total net revenue; 85% of revenue increase), which depends on demand and market price.
- Corporate and investor information: Incorporation (Delaware, 2009), headquarters (San Francisco), websites and investor relations resources, use of social media for disclosures, availability of SEC filings and governance documents; trademark notes.

title: Risk Factors Summary
heading: 1.1 Risk Factors Summary
start_phrase: Our business operations are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including those outside of our control, that could cause our actual results to be harmed, including risks regarding the following:
summary:
- This excerpt is Item 1A. Risk Factors from an annual Form 10-K, warning that investing involves a high degree of risk and that adverse events could materially affect the business and stock price.
- It presents a Risk Factors Summary organized into five categories:
  - Risks related to business and industry: ongoing COVID-19 impacts and participation in government relief programs; brand protection; ability to retain and grow sellers and Cash App customers; investment needs vs. profitability; product and market expansion; pace of innovation in payments/financial services; competitive pressures; global expansion; M&A and other strategic transactions; and Square Capital-specific risks (capital availability, seller repayments, bank partnership structure, product expansion).
  - Operational risks: data misuse or unauthorized access; security breaches and human error; system failures and catastrophic events; custody risks for bitcoin (private keys, hacks, data loss); adequacy of risk management; dependence on card networks and acquiring processors; reliance on third-party processors and settlement partners; dependence on key personnel and talent retention; effectiveness of internal controls; integration with operating systems and third-party devices; component shortages, tariffs, delays, or discontinuations; and demand forecasting and inventory management.
  - Economic, financial, and tax risks: macroeconomic deterioration; higher-than-expected tax liabilities or valuation allowances; limited or costly financing and covenant constraints; ability to service convertible senior notes; and counterparty risk related to convertible note hedge transactions.
  - Legal, regulatory, and compliance risks: extensive regulation across operations; evolving privacy and data protection rules; money transmitter obligations; regulation and scrutiny of Square Financial Services (Utah industrial bank) including source-of-strength requirements; regulation of Cash App Investing (SEC/FINRA) and net capital rules; potential FINRA-imposed business practice changes; litigation and government investigations; intellectual property protection challenges; and volatility/impairment risks tied to bitcoin investments.
  - Risks related to ownership of common stock: dual-class share structure; Class A stock price volatility; impacts of convertible note hedge and warrant transactions; anti-takeover provisions in charter/bylaws and Delaware law; and exclusive forum bylaw provisions.
- The section then expands on COVID-19-specific risks: significant macroeconomic uncertainty; outsized impact on small-business sellers; effects of government restrictions (lockdowns, travel bans) driving unemployment and reduced spending; operational disruptions (e.g., reduced Cash App support due to vendor shutdowns); shifts to remote work and curtailed travel/events; and high uncertainty around duration, vaccine efficacy/distribution, and recovery timeline, with potential lasting impacts such as tighter credit, customer insolvencies, and recessionary pressures.

title: The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and measures intended to prevent its spread have had, and may continue to have, a material and adverse effect on our business and results of operations.
heading: 1.2.1 The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and measures intended to prevent its spread have had, and may continue to have, a material and adverse effect on our business and results of operations.
start_phrase: Global health concerns relating to the COVID-19 pandemic and related government actions taken to reduce the spread of the virus have been weighing on the macroeconomic environment,
summary:
- Highlights extensive legal, regulatory, and compliance exposure across the business, including privacy and data protection, money transmitter obligations, and oversight of key subsidiaries: Square Financial Services (a Utah industrial bank with “source of financial strength” obligations) and Cash App Investing (SEC-registered, FINRA member with net capital and other requirements), as well as potential FINRA-driven changes to business practices.
- Notes litigation risks (including intellectual property claims, government investigations, and regulatory disputes), challenges protecting IP, and volatility/impairment risk tied to bitcoin investments.
- Outlines ownership-related risks: dual-class share structure, Class A stock price volatility, impacts of convertible note hedge and warrant transactions, anti-takeover provisions in corporate documents and Delaware law, and exclusive forum bylaw provisions.
- Details COVID-19 impacts: macroeconomic weakness and uncertainty, disproportionate harm to small-business sellers, operational disruptions (e.g., reduced customer support capacity, remote work, travel and event restrictions), and the unpredictable duration, severity, and aftereffects (credit availability, bankruptcies, recession).
- Describes participation in government relief programs, especially PPP lending via Square Capital (including second-draw eligibility, two- or five-year 1% loans, forgiveness criteria), with approximately $857 million facilitated by December 31, 2020; mix of retained and participated loans, and Federal Reserve borrowing secured by PPP loans; plans to continue participating.
- Explains PPP-related risks: evolving and untested program requirements; potential errors in documentation, verification, forgiveness, and servicing; risk of SBA denying guarantees or forgiveness; underwriting scrutiny; potential losses, litigation, and reputational harm.
- Covers facilitation of stimulus and unemployment payments through Cash App (direct deposit via account/routing numbers, cash-in from state prepaid cards, expanded direct deposit eligibility), and associated heightened risks of fraud, data breaches, technical issues, and resulting operational, compliance, legal, reputational, and governmental enforcement exposure.
text:
The
 ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and measures intended to prevent its spread have had, and may continue to have, a material and adverse effect on ourbusiness and results of operations.
Global health concerns relating to
 the COVID-19 pandemic and related government actions taken to reduce the spread of the virus have been weighing onthe
 macroeconomic environment, and the pandemic has significantly increased economic uncertainty and reduced economic activity. Small businesses, whichconstitute
 a large part of our sellers, have been impacted particularly hard. The pandemic has resulted in government authorities and businesses implementingnumerous
 measures to try to contain the virus, such as travel bans and restrictions, quarantines, shelter in place or total lock-down orders, school closures, andbusiness
 limitations and shutdowns. Such measures have contributed significantly to increased unemployment and negatively impacted consumer and businessspending.
The
 pandemic has adversely impacted, and is likely to continue to adversely impact, our operations and the operations of our customers and businesspartners. For example, our customer supp
ort for Cash App was operating at reduced levels for some time, as certain vendors we had used to perform such functionshad
 to shut down some operations. The pandemic has caused us to modify our business practices to help minimize the risk of the virus to our employees, ourcustomers,
 and the communities in which we participate, which could negatively impact our business. These measures include temporarily requiring employees towork
 remotely, suspending all non-essential business travel for our employees, limiting external guests visiting our offices, and canceling, postponing, or holdingmeetings and
 events virtually. Given the continually evolving situation, there is no certainty that the measures we have taken will be sufficient to mitigate the risksposed by the virus.
The
 extent to which the COVID-19 pandemic impacts our business, results of operations, and financial condition will depend on developments thatcontinue to be
 highly uncertain and difficult to predict, including, but not limited to, the duration and spread of the pandemic, its severity, the actions to contain thevirus
 or treat its impact, the availability, distribution and efficacy of vaccines, and how quickly and to what extent normal economic and operating conditions canresume.
 Even after the COVID-19 pandemic has subsided, we may experience material and adverse impacts to our business as a result of the virus’s globaleconomic impact, inc
luding the availability of credit, bankruptcies or insolvencies of customers, and recession or economic downturn.There
 are no comparable recent events that provide guidance as to the effect the COVID-19 pandemic may have, and, as a result, the ultimate impact ofthe pandemic is highly unce
rtain and subject to change. We do not yet know the full extent of the impacts on our business, our operations, or the global economy asa whole. However, the effects cou
ld have a18
material impact on our results of operations and heighten many of the known risks described throughout this Risk Factors section.

title: Our participation in government relief programs set up in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, such as facilitating loans to businesses under the Paycheck Protection Program or unemployment benefits and stimulus payments to individuals through Cash App, may subject us to new risks and uncertainties.
heading: 1.2.2 Our participation in government relief programs set up in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, such as facilitating loans to businesses under the Paycheck Protection Program or unemployment benefits and stimulus payments to individuals through Cash App, may subject us to new risks and uncertainties.
start_phrase: Federal, state, local, and foreign governmental authorities have enacted, and may enact in the future, legislation, regulations, and programs in response to the COVID-19 pandemic intended to provide economic relief to businesses and individuals.
summary:
- Overview of COVID-19-related risk factors, noting potential material impacts on operations and the amplification of known risks due to participation in government relief programs.
- Square Capital’s role in the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP): approved participant status; program extension to March 31, 2021 with an additional $284B; loan terms (1% fixed rate; two- or five-year terms; up to 2.5x payroll, or 3.5x for qualifying restaurants); forgiveness criteria (use on eligible expenses, at least 60% for payroll, employment maintenance).
- Second-draw PPP eligibility: fewer than 300 employees, at least a 25% revenue decline in any 2020 quarter vs. the same 2019 quarter, and full use of the first PPP loan.
- Operational footprint and funding: approximately $857M in PPP loans facilitated as of December 31, 2020; mix of retained loans and sold participations; borrowing from the Federal Reserve secured by PPP loans; plans to retain second-round PPP loans and continue accessing Fed funding.
- PPP-related risks: evolving and untested processes; documentation, verification, forgiveness, and servicing challenges; exposure if the SBA declines guarantees or forgiveness due to errors or noncompliance; heightened scrutiny of underwriting and documentation; potential losses, litigation, and reputational harm; possible negative impact on business and results.
- Cash App’s facilitation of federal stimulus and unemployment payments: enabling direct deposits via account/routing numbers, accepting deposits from state-issued prepaid cards, and working with partner banks to expand direct deposit eligibility.
- Risks from facilitating stimulus/unemployment payments: increased susceptibility to fraud, data breaches, and technical issues due to rapid, complex program implementation; resulting operational, compliance, legal, and reputational risks, with potential for governmental action, litigation, and material adverse losses.
text:
Federal,
 state, local, and foreign governmental authorities have enacted, and may enact in the future, legislation, regulations, and programs in response tothe COVID-19 pandemic intende
d to provide economic relief to businesses and individuals. Our participation in, or facilitation of, such programs may expose us tonew risks and uncertainties.
Square
 Capital is an approved participant under the Paycheck Protection Program (“PPP”) administered by the Small Business Administration (“SBA”)and
 enacted in March 2020 under the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act ("CARES Act") in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Recently, thePPP
 was extended until March 31, 2021 and an additional $284 billion was allocated to fund a second round of PPP loans. The PPP was intended to providefunding
 for businesses so they can retain employees and includes initial loan repayment deferrals and debt forgiveness provisions for eligible borrowers.Additionally,
 borrowers may now qualify for a “second-draw” loan generally under the same terms and conditions as their initial loans. Small businesses whoreceived a PPP loan previously can 
apply for a second loan if they: (i) employ fewer than 300 employees, (ii) experienced at least a 25% decrease in revenue in anyquarter
 in 2020 relative to same quarter in 2019, and (iii) have already used or will use the full amount of their first PPP loan. Under the program, Square Capital,through a bank
 partner (and directly with respect to the second round of PPP loans), provides small businesses two-year or five-year loans at a fixed interest rate ofone
 percent for up to 2.5 times (or 3.5 times with respect to restaurants qualifying for a second PPP loan) the borrower’s monthly payroll expenses. The loan isforgiven
 under the program if the loan proceeds are used for specified expenses, including payroll and benefit costs, rent payments, utilities, and mortgage andcertain
 interest expenses; provided that at least 60% of the loan proceeds are utilized for qualifying payroll costs and the borrower maintains or rehires employeesduring the
 specified periods. As of December 31, 2020, Square Capital had facilitated approximately $857 million of PPP loans, excluding cancelled loans. SquareCapital
 has retained some of these PPP loans in its portfolio, but also sold 100% participation rights in certain PPP loans to an institutional third-party investor. Inaddition,
 Square Capital has borrowed money from the Federal Reserve secured by PPP loans in its portfolio. Square Capital expects to continue to retain PPPloans from the second round of th
e PPP in its portfolio and to continue to access funds from the Federal Reserve secured by such PPP loans.As
 a participant in the PPP, Square Capital is exposed to new risks and uncertainties since certain processes and program requirements are still beingdeveloped, iterated upon, and have not yet been tested, whic
h exposes us to risks related to documentation, verification, forgiveness, and servicing of such loans. Inthe
 event that it is determined that a borrower does not qualify for loan forgiveness or if a borrower defaults on its PPP loan, Square Capital is at risk to the extentthe
 SBA may decline to honor its guarantee or to forgive the loan due to documentation or verification errors, failure to follow regulatory requirements, or lack ofadherence
 to underwriting standards. As a result, Square Capital’s documentation and review and underwriting processes will be subject to scrutiny, and we couldincur
 losses if we fail to comply with the SBA documentation and other requirements. We also may become subject to litigation arising as a result of ourparticipation
 in this program, which could result in significant financial liability or could adversely affect our reputation. There can be no assurance that SquareCapital will be successful in mitigating all of
 the risks associated with the PPP or that this lending will not have a negative impact on Square Capital’s business andresults of operations.
Separately,
 the  CARES  Act  and  the  Consolidated  Appropriations  Act,  2021  provided  for  stimulus  funds,  called  economic  impact  payments,  toindividuals,
 expanded eligibility for unemployment benefits, increased the amount of unemployment insurance benefits, and extended the period for suchpayments.
 Cash App has been facilitating the payment of such stimulus funds and unemployment benefits by offering account and routing numbers that customerscan
 use to deposit such payments directly into their Cash App accounts and accepting cash-in deposits from prepaid cards issued by state governments. Cash Apphas also
 worked with partner banks to expand direct deposit eligibility for its customers. The federal stimulus programs were set up quickly and under difficult andunprecedented
 circumstances and the implementation of these programs at the federal, state, and local levels has been complex and difficult, causing them to bemore susceptible
 to fraud, data breaches, technical difficulties, and other new and uncertain risks. Cash App’s facilitation of unemployment and stimulus paymentsmay
 therefore expose us to operational, compliance, reputational, and legal risks, which could result in governmental action, litigation, or other forms of materialand adverse loss.

title: Our business depends on a strong and trusted brand, and any failure to maintain, protect, and enhance our brand would hurt our business.
heading: 1.2.3 Our business depends on a strong and trusted brand, and any failure to maintain, protect, and enhance our brand would hurt our business.
start_phrase: We have developed a strong and trusted brand that has contributed significantly to the success of our business.

- Dependence on third-party advertising platforms (e.g., Google, Twitter, Facebook) and retail partners for visibility, customer acquisition, and hardware sales; adverse platform changes or inability to maintain partnerships could harm growth and increase costs.

- Recognition that revenue growth has slowed at times and may slow or decline further; growth rates may differ between reporting segments, with Cash App and Seller potentially growing at different paces.
- Customer retention risk due to lack of long-term contracts and relatively low switching costs; usage may drop due to satisfaction levels, pricing/competition, macroeconomic conditions, or reduced end-customer spending (including impacts from events like COVID-19).
- Growth strategy hinges on retaining and expanding usage among existing sellers and Cash App customers, acquiring new customers (including larger sellers), and successfully launching innovative products and services.
- Importance of increasing Cash App monthly transacting active customers and deepening their engagement as a key driver of long-term financial performance.

title: We have generated significant net losses in the past, and we intend to continue to invest substantially in our business. Thus, we may not be able to maintain profitability.
heading: 1.2.5 We have generated significant net losses in the past, and we intend to continue to invest substantially in our business. Thus, we may not be able to maintain profitability.
start_phrase: While we generated net income of $213.1 million and $375.4 million for the years ended December 31, 2020 and 2019, respectively, we generated net losses of $38.5 million for the year ended December 31, 2018.
summary:

- Continued investment in the Square platform to add or improve features may not succeed; unsuccessful initiatives could slow or reduce growth.
- Profitability is uncertain: despite recent net income, the company has an accumulated deficit and plans substantial ongoing investments (hiring, sales/marketing, product development, acquisitions, infrastructure, international expansion, and compliance) that could raise expenses faster than revenue.
- Costs to acquire/support new or larger sellers and Cash App customers, including higher third-party advertising fees, may increase significantly; upfront seller costs versus deferred revenue recognition can lead to near-term losses.
- The company may make decisions that hurt short-term results in pursuit of long-term benefits, which may not meet investor expectations or materialize, potentially harming the business.
- Efforts to broaden products and services and enter new markets may fail to generate or sustain revenue; acceptance in new markets is uncertain.
- Offerings face technological, operational, and regulatory risks; service disruptions or failures could materially and adversely affect the business.
- Cash App investing features (bitcoin, stocks, ETFs) expose customers to market volatility; customer losses may drive churn and damage brand and reputation.
- New initiatives may not yield growth or timely returns and require significant management attention, potentially limiting growth and harming reputation.

title: Our long-term success depends on our ability to develop products and services to address the rapidly evolving market for payments and financial services, and, if we are not able to implement successful enhancements and new features for our products and services, our business could be materially and adversely affected.
heading: 1.2.7 Our long-term success depends on our ability to develop products and services to address the rapidly evolving market for payments and financial services, and, if we are not able to implement successful enhancements and new features for our products and services, our business could be materially and adversely affected.

- Development efforts may be constrained by industry standards, payment network rules, laws and regulations, customer resistance to change, and third-party intellectual property rights.
- The company depends partly on third parties—including competitors—for access to new technologies and market development; failure to anticipate or respond to industry shifts could impair the business.
- Products must interoperate with diverse systems, infrastructures, and devices and be tailored to customer needs; inability to maintain compatibility or meet requirements could reduce demand and harm customer satisfaction.

- Many competitors have greater resources, larger customer bases, and economies of scale; mergers and acquisitions may strengthen them further.
- Long-standing exclusive relationships between sellers and competitors, and stronger brand trust in competing services, can limit customer acquisition and differentiation.
- Pricing pressures, including competitors’ cross-subsidization, may force price reductions and customized favorable terms, compressing gross profit; the company negotiates discounts and incentives with large sellers.

title: Substantial and increasingly intense competition in our industry may harm our business.
heading: 1.2.8 Substantial and increasingly intense competition in our industry may harm our business.
start_phrase: We compete in markets characterized by vigorous competition, changing technology, evolving industry standards, changing customer needs, and frequent introductions of new products and services.
summary:
- The company’s long-term success depends on continuously developing and enhancing products and services to keep pace with rapid technological change in payments and financial services.
- Emerging technologies—omnichannel commerce, contactless/NFC, digital banking, mobile financial apps, cryptocurrencies, and tokenization—could outperform or render current offerings obsolete; adopting them may require significant time and investment with uncertain returns.
- Product development may be constrained by industry standards, card network rules, evolving laws and regulations, customer resistance, and third-party intellectual property rights.
- The company relies partly on third parties, including competitors, for access to new technologies and market development; failing to anticipate or respond to industry shifts could impair the business.
- Maintaining compatibility with diverse systems, infrastructures, and devices requires continuous updates and customization; failures can reduce demand and customer satisfaction.
- The competitive landscape is intense and expected to escalate, including from non-traditional entrants; larger competitors may leverage greater resources, customer bases, and economies of scale, amplified by mergers and acquisitions.
- Long-standing or exclusive seller relationships with competitors and stronger brand trust can hinder customer acquisition; inability to differentiate would adversely affect results.
- Pricing pressures, including competitor cross-subsidization and seller demands for discounts or customized pricing, could force lower prices and increased incentives, reducing gross profit—especially as the mix shifts toward larger sellers.
- Global expansion requires substantial resources and time, with uncertain payback, and introduces risks such as local competition, cultural and language adaptation, IP and data protection challenges, third-party integration, staffing and management complexities, and higher compliance and operational costs.
- International operations add legal and regulatory burdens (payments, data privacy/protection, information security, anti-corruption/AML), trade and sanctions exposure, FX and tax complexity, public health disruptions (e.g., COVID-19), and geopolitical instability; unsuccessful expansion could limit growth.

title: Expanding our business globally could subject us to new challenges and risks.
heading: 1.2.9 Expanding our business globally could subject us to new challenges and risks.
start_phrase: We currently offer our services and products in multiple countries and plan to continue expanding our business further globally.
summary:
- Discounts and incentives used to drive product and service adoption—especially for large sellers—may need to increase, which could compress gross margins.
- The company is expanding globally, which requires significant time, resources, controls, and upfront investment with uncertain or delayed returns.
- Key global expansion risks include:
  - Difficulty attracting sufficient sellers and Cash App customers and misjudging local competitive dynamics.
  - Challenges adapting to local business customs, language, and culture, and higher costs to localize offerings.
  - Greater complexity and cost in protecting intellectual property and sensitive data.
  - Potential lack of acceptance of products/services or need to alter business practices.
  - Dependence on and integration with local third-party providers.
  - Operational hurdles in staffing and managing foreign teams, plus higher travel, infrastructure, legal, and compliance costs.
  - Recruiting and retention challenges and maintaining company culture.
  - Gaining acceptance from industry self-regulatory bodies.
  - Compliance burdens with evolving and potentially conflicting laws on payments, data privacy/protection, information security, anti-corruption/bribery/AML, and taxation across jurisdictions.
  - Exposure to tariffs, sanctions, fines, trade restrictions, and foreign exchange volatility.
  - Heightened exposure to public health crises (e.g., COVID-19) and related governmental/industry responses.
  - Regional economic and political instability and broader geopolitical risks.
- Failure to manage these challenges could undermine the success of global expansion and limit overall business growth.

title: Any acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, joint ventures, divestitures, and other transactions could fail to achieve strategic objectives, disrupt our ongoing operations or result in operating difficulties, liabilities and expenses, harm our business, and negatively impact our results of operations.
heading: 1.2.10 Any acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, joint ventures, divestitures, and other transactions could fail to achieve strategic objectives, disrupt our ongoing operations or result in operating difficulties, liabilities and expenses, harm our business, and negatively impact our results of operations.
start_phrase: In pursuing our business strategy, we routinely conduct discussions and evaluate opportunities for possible acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, joint ventures, divestitures, and other transactions.
summary:
- The company routinely evaluates and pursues acquisitions, strategic investments, new business entries, joint ventures, divestitures, and related transactions, which can divert management attention, incur costs even if not completed, and may fail to meet strategic objectives.
- Key risks of such transactions include difficulties obtaining regulatory approvals; potential for added regulatory burdens; uncertain returns or revenue uplift; significant acquisition and transition costs; and challenges integrating technology, systems, culture, and personnel.
- Additional risks include failure to realize expected synergies on schedule (or at all); inability to retain key talent; undetected liabilities despite due diligence; compliance gaps at acquired firms (including data privacy and security), compounded by complex technology stacks and technical debt.
- Transactions may hinder entry into new market segments or geographies; jeopardize retention of customers, vendors, and partners; trigger lawsuits or regulatory actions; expose the company to security weaknesses or cyber risks of acquired/partner firms; and result in equity dilution or new debt.
- Divestitures can be difficult to execute on acceptable terms, may be hard to separate operationally, can reduce revenue or margins, and might not yield intended strategic or financial benefits.
- Example: Sale of Caviar to DoorDash created exposure to mark-to-market volatility of DoorDash equity, lock-up constraints on selling shares, potential failure to realize value, and ongoing liabilities (including indemnities) and relationship disruptions.
- During divestiture processes, businesses may decline, and employees, customers, or suppliers may be lost; deals may fail to close, leaving sunk costs and uncertainty about finding equivalent buyers.
- Joint ventures and minority investments entail reduced control, higher financial/legal/operational/regulatory risks, dependence on partners with potentially conflicting interests, and potential for actions that harm investment value, invite litigation/regulatory action, or damage brand reputation.
- Square Capital faces specific risks tied to third-party investor demand for loans originated by its bank partner; reduced purchases or pricing/servicing-fee cuts could force scaling back, require company funding, and harm performance; repurchase obligations exist for eligibility breaches.
- Square Capital loans are unsecured; macroeconomic deterioration or weaker seller credit can increase defaults, extend repayment periods, and reduce servicing fees; recourse is limited to the business.
- COVID-19 has heightened risks by reducing eligible sellers, complicating seller identification and risk management for the bank partner, increasing expected losses on owned loans, and elevating non-payment and fraud risks.

title: Square Capital is subject to additional risks relating to the availability of capital, seller payments, availability and structure of its bank partnership, expansion of its products, regulatory obligations, and general macroeconomic conditions.
heading: 1.2.11 Square Capital is subject to additional risks relating to the availability of capital, seller payments, availability and structure of its bank partnership, expansion of its products, regulatory obligations, and general macroeconomic conditions.
start_phrase: Square Capital, which includes our wholly owned subsidiary Square Capital, LLC, is subject to risks in addition to those described elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
summary:
- Risks from acquisitions and divestitures: potential equity dilution, new debt, difficulty selling assets on acceptable terms, separation and integration challenges, loss of revenue/margins, and failure to realize strategic/financial benefits. Example: 2019 sale of Caviar to DoorDash created mark-to-market volatility tied to DoorDash’s stock and lock-up constraints, with no assurance of realizing full value. Transactions can delay objectives, add costs, disrupt relationships, and create ongoing obligations (including indemnities). Pending divestitures risk business decline, loss of employees/customers/suppliers, failure to close, and sunk costs.
- Joint ventures and minority investments: reduced control heightens financial, legal, operational, regulatory, and compliance risks; dependence on partners or controlling parties with potentially conflicting goals; partners’ actions can impair investment value, trigger litigation/regulatory action, and harm reputation/brand.
- Square Capital risks: dependence on institutional investors to purchase bank-originated business loans; if investor demand, pricing, or servicing fees fall, originations may drop or the company may need to self-fund or scale back; repurchase obligations for eligibility breaches. Loans are generally unsecured; adverse macroeconomic conditions (including COVID-19) and seller credit deterioration can increase defaults, extend repayment, and reduce servicing fees; elevated losses on owned portfolio. Lending paused (except PPP) in Q2 2020 and resumed in Q3 under stricter criteria with uncertain volumes; underwriting/pricing misestimation could materially harm the business.
- Bank partnership and regulatory exposure: non-exclusive partnership with a Utah-chartered, FDIC-member industrial bank that may offer competing products; subject to FDIC/Utah oversight and third-party vendor examinations. Ongoing scrutiny and litigation of bank–fintech partnered lending models present risk. Loss or unfavorable change of the bank partner, or inability to secure alternatives/state licenses, could be costly, delay operations, reduce investor participation, and adversely affect Square Capital.
- Future models and licensing: exploring additional products/structures, including forming a Utah industrial bank and other credit offerings, which may require new data, procedures, partnerships, licenses, and regulatory approvals; state licensing entails reporting, bonding, and inspections. Failure to expand/evolve successfully or burdensome regulations could impede growth and success of Square Capital.
- Operational/data security risks: the company, sellers, and partners handle large volumes of sensitive data (PII, payment details, bank info, loan data, seller performance), with certain products subject to HIPAA. Reliance on third-party developers, vendors, and a distributed workforce increases exposure. Breaches, ransomware/APT attacks, or bugs—actual or perceived—could lead to unauthorized access or exfiltration of data/funds, damage brand and business, and result in material costs and liabilities.

start_phrase: We, our sellers, and our partners, including third-party vendors and data centers that we use, obtain and process large amounts of sensitive data, including data related to our customers, our sellers’ customers, and their transactions.
summary:
- Square Capital paused regular business lending in Q2 2020 except PPP loans; resumed in Q3 2020 with stricter criteria, with uncertainty around future volumes and credit performance.
- Mispricing or misjudging repayment risk on business loans could materially harm results.
- Lending is originated through a non-exclusive partnership with a Utah-chartered, FDIC-member industrial bank that may also compete with the company; the company is subject to FDIC third-party vendor audits and oversight.
- Partnered-lending models face regulatory scrutiny and litigation risk; loss or deterioration of the bank partnership, or inability to secure alternatives or state licenses, could disrupt lending and deter institutional loan buyers.
- The company may explore new structures, including forming a Utah industrial bank and launching new credit/loan products, which could require additional data, processes, partnerships, licenses, and regulatory approvals; state licensing brings reporting, bonding, and inspections.
- Failure to successfully expand Square Capital or comply with evolving regulations could adversely affect growth and performance.
- Significant operational risks from handling large volumes of sensitive data (PII, financial, loan, and, for some products, HIPAA-regulated health data) across the company, sellers, partners, vendors, and a distributed workforce.
- Exposure to third-party developer apps increases data access risks; breaches, ransomware/APT attacks, or perceived incidents could cause reputational damage, remediation costs, litigation, and regulatory actions.
- Liability under payment card rules for card data breaches by the company, sellers, or third parties; breaches of bitcoin/blockchain ecosystems could also erode trust.
- Cyber insurance may be inadequate or unavailable; large uncovered claims could materially impact financials.
- Risks of software/hardware defects, system errors, security issues, and human error affecting high-volume, complex transaction processing; potential settlement errors, reporting issues, and fee collection impacts.
- Reliance on a limited number of overseas hardware suppliers reduces quality control; defects can trigger recalls, shortages, redesigns, investigations, and lawsuits.

title: Our products and services may not function as intended due to errors in our software, hardware, and systems, product defects, or due to security breaches or human error in administering these systems, which could materially and adversely affect our business.
heading: 1.3.2 Our products and services may not function as intended due to errors in our software, hardware, and systems, product defects, or due to security breaches or human error in administering these systems, which could materially and adversely affect our business.
start_phrase: Our software, hardware, systems, and processes may contain undetected errors or vulnerabilities that could have a material adverse effect on our business, particularly to the extent such errors or vulnerabilities are not detected and remedied quickly.
summary:
- Cybersecurity and data breach risks: Potential for significant financial losses, remediation costs, legal liability, regulatory scrutiny, and investigations; exposure under payment card rules if seller or third-party breaches occur; reputational damage that can hinder customer acquisition and retention; third-party and ecosystem breaches (including bitcoin/blockchain) can have similar reputational effects; cyber insurance may be inadequate or denied, and large claims could exceed coverage.
- Product and service reliability risks: Undetected errors or vulnerabilities in software, hardware, and systems; defects found in customer-facing software/hardware and third-party integrations; reliance on a limited set of overseas suppliers reduces control over product quality; growing complexity and acquisitions increase risk; frequent updates heighten the chance of errors.
- Operational and financial impacts of errors/security incidents: Possible payment settlement delays or errors, oversettlement, reporting mistakes, and loss of transaction fees; unauthorized access to sensitive or confidential data; product safety issues in hardware that could trigger recalls, shortages, redesign costs, regulatory inquiries, litigation, and other liabilities.
- Targeted cyber-attacks: Electronic payment, hardware, and software products are frequent targets; attack techniques evolve rapidly and may be hard to detect or prevent; failure to anticipate or block attacks can harm customers, reputation, and create significant liability.
- System outages and catastrophic event risks: Service interruptions can arise from cyber-attacks, human error, natural disasters, power/telecom failures, pandemics, and geopolitical unrest affecting company and third-party data centers; limited redundancy and disaster recovery not sufficient for all scenarios; heightened regulatory scrutiny of business continuity and disaster recovery for financial services; denial-of-service and other incidents have occurred and likely will continue, causing revenue loss and remediation costs; COVID-19 increased attack surface due to remote work and digital activity; persistent outages can drive customers to competitors and prompt damage claims.
- Geographic and insurance exposure: Headquarters and some data centers in the earthquake-prone San Francisco Bay Area; insurance may not cover significant losses from service disruptions or disasters, potentially leading to material adverse impacts.
- Bitcoin custody risks: Loss, destruction, or compromise of private keys could render bitcoins inaccessible; wallets may be hacked or compromised; inability to access customer-held bitcoins would harm customer trust and the company’s reputation.

heading: 1.3.3 Systems failures, interruptions, delays in service, catastrophic events, and resulting interruptions in the availability of our products or services, or those of our sellers, could harm our business and our brand, and subject us to substantial liability.
start_phrase: Our systems and those of our third-party vendors, including data center facilities, may experience service interruptions, outages, cyber-attacks and security incidents, human error, earthquakes, hurricanes,
summary:
- Heightened cybersecurity risks to electronic payment, hardware, and software products, with evolving attack techniques that are hard to detect or prevent, potentially harming customers, damaging reputation, and creating significant liability.
- Vulnerability to system failures and service interruptions from outages, cyber-attacks, human error, natural disasters, power/telecom disruptions, fraud, geopolitical events, regulatory changes, and physical security incidents (break-ins, sabotage, vandalism).
- Limited system redundancy and disaster-recovery preparedness; increased regulatory scrutiny for business continuity and disaster recovery plans that can be costly and resource-intensive.
- Ongoing exposure to denial-of-service attacks and other incidents leading to revenue loss, repair/remediation costs, and data loss or corruption.
- COVID-19-driven increase in cyber risks due to remote work and growth in online payments and commerce; prolonged or frequent service degradation could cause customer attrition and lasting reputational damage.
- Potential legal claims from customers and counterparties arising from outages or failures, with associated time and cost burdens even if claims are unsuccessful.
- Significant natural or man-made disaster risk, particularly given headquarters and data centers in the seismically active San Francisco Bay Area; possible lengthy service interruptions, related liabilities, and insufficient insurance coverage.
- Adverse impacts on sellers and customers from widespread disasters or pandemics that could negatively affect overall operating results.
- Bitcoin custody risk: loss, destruction, or compromise of private keys (without accessible backup) could render bitcoins inaccessible; risk of wallet hacks; potential harm to customer trust and business.

- Concentration risk from natural or man-made disasters, particularly seismic risk in the San Francisco Bay Area where headquarters and data centers are located; insurance may be insufficient to cover significant service disruption losses.
- Bitcoin custody and private key risks: loss, destruction, or compromise of private keys (or wallet hacks) could irreversibly block access to customer bitcoins, erode trust, require significant remediation spend, and expose the company to litigation and liability; broader crypto ecosystem breaches can also harm reputation; growing bitcoin balances amplify consequences.
- Potential ineffectiveness of risk management programs to vet customers and transactions, with exposure to fraud, scams, money laundering, and terrorist financing, especially given highly automated/liquid payment and P2P services.
- Scaling, product expansion (e.g., online acceptance, consumer financing, loans), and entry into new markets increase difficulty forecasting fraud losses and setting reserves; COVID-19 and growth place additional strain on compliance and risk infrastructure.
- Insurance coverage gaps and selective self-insurance may leave the company exposed to certain risks and expenses.
- Chargeback and refund exposure: higher risk for sellers with future delivery obligations and during economic downturns; inability to recover from insolvent or closed sellers results in losses borne by the company as merchant of record; limited reserves may not fully mitigate losses.
- EMV liability shift increases seller responsibility for certain fraud when not using EMV-compliant readers; not all offered readers are EMV-compliant, raising reimbursement needs and the risk of fines or penalties from payment networks if chargeback losses exceed acceptable levels.

title: Our risk management efforts may not be effective, which could expose us to losses and liability and otherwise harm our business.
heading: 1.3.5 Our risk management efforts may not be effective, which could expose us to losses and liability and otherwise harm our business.
start_phrase: We offer payments and other products and services to a large number of customers.
summary:
- Security risks related to cryptocurrencies and blockchain: potential hacks, loss of private keys, and compromises of digital wallets (both customer and third-party) could block access to funds, damage trust, trigger remediation costs and litigation, and create reputational harm; risk grows as customer bitcoin balances increase.
- Limitations of risk management: challenges in detecting and preventing fraud and illegitimate transactions; increased exposure from larger sellers; potential regulatory enforcement and partner contract breaches; susceptibility of payments and peer-to-peer services to scams, identity theft, money laundering, and terrorist financing; need for ongoing enhancement amid COVID-19 impacts and expansion; difficulty forecasting losses for new services/markets; partial reliance on self-insurance and limited insurance coverage.
- Chargeback and refund exposure: higher risk with future-delivery sellers and during economic downturns; insolvency or bankruptcy of sellers can shift losses to the company as merchant of record; limited reserves may not cover losses; EMV liability shift increases reimbursement demands on non-EMV sellers; potential fines, higher fees, or loss of card-processing ability if chargeback losses are not controlled.
- Dependence on payment card networks and acquiring processors: reliance on Visa, MasterCard, American Express, Discover, and third-party banks/processors; risks from contract expirations, unfavorable renewals, service degradation, or preferential treatment for competitors; mandatory compliance with evolving network operating rules (including payment facilitator rules) with potential fines or processing bans for violations; possible loss of incentives and increased costs.
- Fee and pricing risks: obligation to pay interchange, assessments, processing, and settlement fees that networks may increase or regulators may alter; favorable pricing often contingent on business conditions; standard-rate pricing model exposes margins and competitiveness to fee changes; peer-to-peer costs could rise if network fees increase.
- Penalties for high-risk or illegal seller activity: responsibility to prevent or register and monitor high-risk sellers; failure can result in material penalties, required onboarding process changes, or termination of card acceptance.

title: We are dependent on payment card networks and acquiring processors, and any changes to their rules or practices could harm our business.
heading: 1.3.6 We are dependent on payment card networks and acquiring processors, and any changes to their rules or practices could harm our business.
start_phrase: Our business depends on our ability to accept credit and debit cards, and this ability is provided by the payment card networks, including Visa, MasterCard, American Express, and Discover.
summary:
- The company’s business depends on accepting credit and debit cards via payment card networks (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover) and third‑party banks/acquiring processors; disruptions, unfavorable renewals, or preferential treatment of competitors by these partners could harm operations.
- Acquiring processor agreements are time‑limited (major ones expiring between Q3 2022 and Q1 2023), and counterparties could refuse to process transactions adequately, breach terms, or impose added costs/requirements.
- Payment card networks can change or reinterpret operating rules at any time, including payment facilitator rules and chargeback standards; noncompliance can lead to fines, loss of incentives, increased costs, mandated operational changes, or termination of card acceptance.
- Rising interchange, assessment, processing, and bank settlement fees—whether from network decisions, missed pricing conditions, or regulation—could compress margins, force pricing model changes, or reduce competitiveness, particularly because seller pricing often does not pass through these fees directly; similar fee increases could affect peer‑to‑peer transactions on Cash App.
- Ineffective risk management (e.g., self‑insurance, seller reserves) could lead to significant financial losses and potential civil or criminal liability.
- Failure to detect or properly manage high‑risk or illegal seller activity can trigger network penalties, require enhanced monitoring/registration of such sellers, and potentially jeopardize the ability to accept payment cards.
- Overall, any material limitations on card acceptance or increases in transaction‑based fees would adversely affect the company’s business and financial results.

title: We rely on third parties and their systems for a variety of services, including the processing of transaction data and settlement of funds to us and our sellers, and these third parties’ failure to perform these services adequately could materially and adversely affect our business.
heading: 1.3.7 We rely on third parties and their systems for a variety of services, including the processing of transaction data and settlement of funds to us and our sellers, and these third parties’ failure to perform these services adequately could materially and adversely affect our business.
start_phrase: To provide our products and services, we rely on third parties that we do not control, such as the payment card networks, our acquiring and issuing processors, the payment card issuers, a carrying broker, various financial institution partners, systems like the Federal Reserve Automated Clearing House, and other partners.
summary:
- Heavy reliance on third-party financial networks and partners (payment card networks, acquiring/issuing processors, card issuers, brokers, banks, and ACH/Fed systems) for core services like transaction transmission, chargebacks/refunds, settlements, and brokerage; a limited set of acquiring processors by region increases concentration risk.
- Operational and financial exposure if these third parties experience outages, errors, insolvency, or impose unfavorable terms; switching providers could be costly and disruptive. The company has previously experienced third-party outages that affected branded card processing.
- Dependence on key executives and skilled employees; loss of leadership or key personnel could disrupt operations. Jack Dorsey’s dual CEO role may constrain his availability.
- Intense competition for talent, especially in the San Francisco Bay Area, may require significant cash and equity to attract/retain employees; immigration policy changes could hinder hiring and international operations.
- Need to continually enhance infrastructure, internal controls, and reporting to manage growth and new business lines; priorities include upgrading administrative systems, installing stronger management information and control systems, and preserving and communicating core values and strategies globally.
- Failure to recruit/retain talent or to improve operational and financial systems could materially harm business performance and growth prospects.

title: We depend on key management, as well as our experienced and capable employees, and any failure to attract, motivate, and retain our employees could harm our ability to maintain and grow our business.
heading: 1.3.8 We depend on key management, as well as our experienced and capable employees, and any failure to attract, motivate, and retain our employees could harm our ability to maintain and grow our business.
start_phrase: Our future success is significantly dependent upon the continued service of our executives and other key employees.
summary:
- Dependence on third-party providers: The company relies on payment networks, acquiring and issuing processors, card issuers, a carrying broker, financial institution partners, and systems like the Federal Reserve ACH for core functions such as transaction transmission, chargebacks/refunds, fund settlement, brokerage, and data services. Transitioning providers could be disruptive and costly. Failures, outages, errors, insolvency, or unfavorable terms from these third parties could materially and adversely affect operations; the company has experienced third‑party outages impacting branded card payments.
- Concentration of acquiring processors: Relies on three acquiring processors in the U.S., Canada, and Japan, and two in Australia and the U.K., heightening transition and continuity risks.
- Talent and leadership risks: Success depends on retaining executives and key employees; loss of such personnel could disrupt operations and increase costs. The CEO’s concurrent role at another company may limit time and focus. Recruiting and retaining highly skilled talent is competitive and costly, especially in the San Francisco Bay Area, and returns on such investments are uncertain.
- Immigration and global staffing constraints: Potential changes to U.S. and other countries’ immigration/visa policies may hinder hiring, renewals, or project staffing, adversely affecting international expansion and overall operations.
- Scaling and internal controls: Rapid growth and new business lines place significant demands on management and resources. The company must strengthen infrastructure, operational procedures, internal controls, and reporting systems to manage growth effectively. Key challenges include improving administrative infrastructure (operational, financial, communications systems), installing enhanced management information/control systems, and preserving and communicating core values, strategies, and goals across a global workforce.

title: If we do not continue to improve our operational, financial, and other internal controls and systems to manage growth effectively, our business could be harmed.
heading: 1.3.9 If we do not continue to improve our operational, financial, and other internal controls and systems to manage growth effectively, our business could be harmed.
start_phrase: Our current business and anticipated growth, as well as our entry into new lines of business, will continue to place significant demands on our management and other resources.
summary:
- Heavy reliance on third parties (payment networks, acquiring/issuing processors, card issuers, financial institutions, ACH systems, brokers, app marketplaces) for core services such as transaction transmission, chargebacks/refunds, fund settlement, and brokerage; limited numbers of processors per region increase concentration risk. Failures, outages, errors, unfavorable terms, or insolvency of these partners—and disruptions when adding or switching providers—could materially and adversely affect operations; past third‑party outages have already impacted card processing.

- Dependence on key executives and skilled employees; challenges in attracting, motivating, and retaining talent amid intense competition (especially in the Bay Area), potential immigration/visa constraints, and management transitions. Loss of key leaders (including time commitments of the CEO) or inability to hire/retain talent could disrupt operations, increase costs, and hinder growth and strategic execution.

- Need to scale and strengthen operational, financial, and internal control systems to manage rapid growth and new business lines. Risks include delays in implementing infrastructure and management information systems, difficulty preserving core values and alignment, and reduced agility in launching features and responding to market needs. Failure to implement effective processes and tools could impair competitiveness and business objectives.

- Product interoperability risks: services must work across diverse, third‑party operating systems and browsers; changes by platform owners (including Apple and Google) or app marketplace policies/updates could degrade functionality, add costs, favor competitors, or hinder app distribution and access, negatively impacting usage and customer satisfaction.

- Hardware compatibility risks: readers depend on third‑party mobile device interfaces (e.g., audio jack, Lightning). Changes in device design or connection standards may require costly hardware/software modifications; inability or merchant reluctance to adapt could reduce demand and harm the business.

- Supply chain concentration risks: many key components and manufacturing services are single‑ or limited‑sourced, with limited firm commitments and custom tooling held by manufacturers. Exposure to shortages, long lead times, price increases, tariffs, design changes, delays, or discontinuations may disrupt production. Alternative supplier qualification efforts may not succeed, which could materially and adversely affect product availability and costs.

title: Our services must integrate with a variety of operating systems, and the hardware that enables merchants to accept payment cards must interoperate with third-party mobile devices utilizing those operating systems. If we are unable to ensure that our services or hardware interoperate with such operating systems and devices, our business may be materially and adversely affected.

If we are unable to ensure that our services or hardware interoperate with such operating systems and devices, our business may be materially and adversely affected.
start_phrase: We are dependent on the ability of our products and services to integrate with a variety of operating systems, as well as web browsers, that we do not control.
summary:
- Growth and operational scalability risk: The company must develop robust processes and tools to manage a growing enterprise, requiring significant investments. Balancing added controls with rapid feature development may slow innovation relative to smaller competitors. Failure to effectively manage growth could impair business performance.

- Dependence on third-party platforms and ecosystems: Products and services must interoperate with multiple operating systems, web browsers, and third-party mobile devices. Changes by platform owners (e.g., Apple, Google) or their app marketplaces—such as policy shifts, software updates, or preferential treatment of competing services—can degrade functionality, increase costs, reduce accessibility, and harm usage.

- Hardware compatibility challenges: Company hardware relies on device interfaces (e.g., audio jack, Lightning). Changes in connectors or device designs may require costly modifications or additional parts, and merchant reluctance to adopt such changes could adversely affect the business.

- Concentrated supply chain exposure: Many key components and manufacturing services are single- or limited-sourced, with some reliance on a single manufacturer for assembly and custom-tooled parts. Agreements often auto-renew but lack firm commitments on volumes or timelines. This creates risks of shortages, delays, price increases, tariffs, or discontinuations, and efforts to qualify alternative suppliers may not succeed.

- Overall impact: Any of these factors could materially and adversely affect product performance, customer satisfaction, and the company’s business.

heading: 1.3.11 Many of our key components are procured from a single or limited number of suppliers. Thus, we are at risk of shortage, price increases, tariffs, changes, delay, or discontinuation of key components, which could disrupt and materially and adversely affect our business.
start_phrase: Many of the key components used to manufacture our products, such as the custom parts of our magstripe reader come from limited or single sources of supply.
summary:
- Challenges of scaling: Need to implement effective processes, controls, and tools while maintaining agility; risk that growth slows feature delivery and market responsiveness, impairing competitiveness.
- Platform and OS dependencies: Services and hardware must interoperate with multiple operating systems, browsers, and third-party mobile devices; platform changes, added requirements, or preferential treatment of competitors could degrade functionality and demand.
- App marketplace reliance: Dependence on Apple App Store and Google Play; marketplace policy or design changes and software updates can hinder access, break compatibility, reduce downloads, and harm customer satisfaction.
- Hardware interoperability risks: Changes to device interfaces (e.g., audio jack, Lightning) and wireless/wired standards may require costly hardware/software modifications; merchants may resist added accessories, affecting adoption.
- Supplier concentration: Many key components and manufacturing are single- or limited-sourced; limited commitments from contract manufacturers; risk of shortages, long lead times, discontinuations, or price increases.
- Supply chain disruptions: Potential issues from equipment failures, labor shortages/strikes, natural disasters, disease outbreaks (notably COVID-19), cost spikes, insolvency, regulatory changes, trade restrictions, and logistics incidents (e.g., port shutdowns, damage in transit, IP theft, tampering, vendor quality/compliance failures).
- COVID-19 impacts: Ongoing supply chain disruptions, hardware shortages, restricted travel affecting prototype development, and negative effects on seller acquisition and financial results.
- Tariffs and trade policy: U.S. tariffs on China-manufactured hardware (10% rising to 25%, additional 15% later reduced to 7.5%) have pressured gross margins; future tariffs or restrictions could further harm pricing competitiveness and financial performance.
- Demand forecasting and inventory management: Long lead-time investments (e.g., Square Reader) require accurate forecasts; underestimation leads to shortages, overestimation to excess/obsolete inventory, write-downs, discounted sales, and gross margin erosion; demand volatility includes COVID-19-related impacts.
- Overall risk: These factors could materially and adversely affect product availability, customer relationships, growth, profitability, financial condition, and results of operations.

title: A deterioration of general macroeconomic conditions could materially and adversely affect our business and financial results.
heading: 1.4.1 A deterioration of general macroeconomic conditions could materially and adversely affect our business and financial results.
start_phrase: Our performance is subject to economic conditions and their impact on levels of spending by businesses and individuals.
summary:
- Focus on economic, financial, and tax risks that could materially and adversely affect the business.
- Heavy dependence on small-business sellers, who are disproportionately vulnerable to economic downturns and COVID-19 impacts, leading to reduced sales, fewer processed payments, higher failure rates, and potential cessation of service use.
- Potential increases in transaction and advance loss rates, exposure to chargebacks after sellers cease operations, and negative effects on the Square Capital program (slower growth in qualified sellers, slower repayments, or defaults); similar vulnerability for consumer financing customers.
- Financial stress among suppliers, distributors, and third-party partners (pricing pressure, delayed payments, insolvency) that could hinder meeting customer demand and revenue collection.
- Investment portfolio exposure to credit, liquidity, market, and interest rate risks; prolonged market declines or downgrades could trigger impairment charges and hurt financial results.
- COVID-19-related uncertainties and restrictions causing lasting economic effects, including risks tied to office lease obligations and challenges subletting unused space due to work-from-home practices.
- Brexit-related economic and legal uncertainty, with the risk of divergent laws, regulations, and licensing requirements adversely affecting operations and results.
- Exposure to greater-than-anticipated tax liabilities across multiple jurisdictions; risk from audits and disputes with tax authorities, exemplified by a $38 million Texas sales and use tax assessment (including interest and penalties) over classification of services.

title: We may have exposure to greater-than-anticipated tax liabilities, which may materially and adversely affect our business.
heading: 1.4.2 We may have exposure to greater-than-anticipated tax liabilities, which may materially and adversely affect our business.
start_phrase: We are subject to income taxes and non-income taxes in the United States and other countries in which we transact or conduct business, and such laws and rates vary by jurisdiction.
summary:
- The company is highly sensitive to macroeconomic downturns, which reduce business and consumer spending and disproportionately impact its small-business sellers, leading to lower payment volumes, higher chargebacks after seller closures, elevated transaction and advance loss rates, and slower or non-repayment in programs like Square Capital; consumer financing customers may also be more prone to default.
- COVID-19 has created enduring economic uncertainty and operational impacts (e.g., reduced seller activity, travel and business restrictions), including potential costs from excess leased office space due to remote work and difficulties subletting.
- Suppliers, distributors, and third-party partners may face financial stress (pricing demands, delayed payments, insolvency), disrupting operations and revenue collection.
- The investment portfolio faces credit, liquidity, market, and interest rate risks; prolonged market declines or downgrades could trigger impairments and harm financial results.
- Brexit may introduce legal and regulatory divergence in the UK and EU, increasing uncertainty, compliance complexity, and potential operational and financial impacts.
- Significant tax risk exposure: the company is subject to audits and may face disagreements with tax authorities across jurisdictions; example cited is a $38 million Texas sales and use tax assessment that the company disputes, with potential for additional liabilities, interest, and penalties if unsuccessful; reserves may be insufficient.
- Evolving tax laws and practices (including OECD/EU initiatives) could change long-standing principles and broaden taxable activities (e.g., internet hosting, data processing, telecommunications), increasing tax burdens and compliance costs.
- New or expanded taxes (sales & use, VAT, digital services, income) and obligations on marketplaces/payment providers to collect and remit taxes may raise costs, add reporting/record-keeping requirements, and expose the company to penalties and business restrictions for noncompliance.
- Determining global tax provisions is complex and judgment-based; outcomes may differ from estimates and materially affect results.
- The company maintains valuation allowances on deferred tax assets and may adjust them over time; increases or releases could materially impact and cause volatility in quarterly and annual results.

 for $38 million, including interest and penalties, following its sales and use tax audit for the period starting January 1, 2015 through April 30, 2018.The Comptroller alleges that services that

 While we have established reserves based on assumptions and estimates that we believe are reasonably sufficient to cover such eventualities, anyadverse outcome of such a r
eview or audit could have an adverse impact on our financial position and results of operations if the reserves prove to be insufficient.Our
 tax liability could be adversely affected by changes in tax laws, rates, regulations, and administrative practices. Our income tax obligations are basedon

 tax principles, which could adversely affect our effective tax rate. Additionally, tax authorities at the international, federal, state, and local levels arecurrently reviewing the appropriate tax treatment of companies engaged in internet commerce and financial technology and attempting to broaden the classification
and

iness.The
