title: Hardware revenue
heading: 1.9.1.4.3 Hardware revenue
start_phrase:
The
 Company generates revenue through the sale of hardware through e-commerce and through its retail distribution channels.
summary:
- Overview of revenue recognition policies across multiple offerings under ASC 606, including timing, performance obligations, billing practices, and variable consideration.
- Loans sold to third-party investors:
  - Company purchases loans from a partner bank and records net amounts paid as loan cost.
  - Recognizes gain on sale as revenue upon transfer of title to third-party investors.
  - Retained loan servicing generates servicing fees recognized as services are delivered through managed payments solutions.
  - For loans not immediately sold, recognizes revenue from expected seller repayments over loan cost proportionate to principal reduction.
- Website hosting and domain registration:
  - Fees generally billed at inception.
  - Performance obligations satisfied over time; revenue recognized ratably over contract terms (hosting: 1–24 months; domains: 1–10 years).
- SaaS subscriptions:
  - Monthly term contracts with automatic renewals; invoiced monthly.
  - Revenue recognized ratably over each month as services are provided.
- Caviar (food ordering platform; sold Oct 31, 2019):
  - Performance obligations: delivery of food orders to customers and catered meals to corporate clients.
  - Fees charged to restaurants (sellers), individuals (delivery/service fees), and corporate customers (catering).
  - Billed upon delivery; revenue recognized upon delivery net of estimated refunds based on historical experience.
- Hardware revenue:
  - Recognized upon delivery to end users, distributors, and retailers via e-commerce and retail channels.
  - Returns treated as variable consideration, estimated from historical data and reducing recognized revenue.
  - Payment terms: end users due upon invoicing; distributors/retailers 30–90 days.
  - Hardware installment sales (3–24 months): allocate and recognize significant financing component as financing revenue within subscription and services over the arrangement term; practical expedient applied for terms of one year or less.
- Bitcoin revenue (Cash App):
  - Revenue recognized when bitcoin is transferred to the customer’s account.
  - Company purchases bitcoin from private broker-dealers or customers, applies a margin, records sales on a gross basis with bitcoin cost in cost of revenues.
  - Treated as principal due to control prior to delivery, primary responsibility for delivery, exposure to price fluctuations, and pricing discretion.

start_phrase:

Uncertain tax positions are recognized when more likely than not to be sustained and measured as the largest amount with greater than 50% likelihood of realization; related interest and penalties are recorded in income tax expense.

 on the recoverability of deferred tax assets. The Company’s judgment regarding future profitability contains significant assumptions and estimates offuture
 operations. If such assumptions were to differ significantly from actual future results of operations, it may have a material impact on the Company’s abilityto
 realize its deferred tax assets. At the end of each period, the Company assesses the ability to realize the deferred tax assets. If it is more likely than not that theCompany would not realize the de
ferred tax assets, then the Company would establish a valuation allowance for all or a portion of the deferred tax assets.The
 Company recognizes the effect of uncertain income tax positions only if those positions are more likely than not of being sustained. Recognizedincome
 tax positions are measured at the largest amount that has a greater than 50% likelihood of being realized. Changes in recognition or measurement arereflected
 in the period in which the change in judgment occurs. The Company records interest and penalties related to uncertain tax positions in the provision forincome tax expense on the conso
lidated statements of operations.

title: Cash and Cash Equivalents and Restricted Cash
heading: 1.9.1.11 Cash and Cash Equivalents and Restricted Cash
start_phrase:
The Company considers all highly liquid investment
s, including money market funds, with an original maturity of three months or less when purchased tobe cash equivalents.
summary:
- Share-based compensation: Options valued using the Black‑Scholes‑Merton model. Key assumptions include expected term (using the simplified method averaging vesting and contractual terms), expected volatility (historical; switched to using the Company’s own stock volatility starting May 2020, no longer using peers), risk‑free Treasury rates, and expected dividends. Expense recognized on a straight‑line basis over service period; forfeitures accounted for as they occur.
- Interest income and expense: Interest income from marketable debt securities and interest expense from long‑term debt, with specific amounts disclosed for 2018–2020 (income: $19.8m, $23.4m, $18.3m; expense: $37.8m, $44.9m, $75.2m).
- Income taxes: Asset‑and‑liability method for deferred taxes; recognition of deferred tax assets/liabilities based on enacted rates and temporary differences, NOLs, and credits. Valuation allowance recorded to the extent deferred tax assets are not more likely than not to be realized, based on history, planning strategies, timing of reversals, and projections. Uncertain tax positions recognized only if more‑likely‑than‑not, measured at the largest amount with >50% likelihood; related interest and penalties recorded in tax expense.
- Cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash: Cash equivalents include highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less. Restricted cash balances disclosed for 2019–2020, primarily to secure letters of credit for payment processing timing differences and as collateral for a loan product with an originating bank (current) and for multi‑year lease agreements (non‑current), with classification based on expected restriction period.
- Concentration of credit risk: No single customer >10% of revenue for 2018–2020. Settlements receivable concentrated among a small number of third‑party payment processors with stated percentages by year; settlement typically occurs within 1–2 business days. Concentration risks for cash, restricted cash, marketable securities, settlements receivable, customer funds, and loans held for sale are mitigated through creditworthy institutions, diversification, credit evaluations, and monitoring; PPP loan risk reduced due to government guarantees.
- Investments in marketable debt securities: Portfolio includes government/agency securities, corporate bonds, commercial paper, and municipal securities. Classified as available‑for‑sale, carried at fair value with unrealized gains/losses (net of tax) in equity (OCI). Securities are highly rated; the Company has the ability and intent to hold positions with unrealized losses to recovery or maturity. Realized gains/losses recognized in other expense (income), net, using specific identification.
- Investments in equity securities: Holdings without control or significant influence. Marketable equities measured at fair value with changes in other expense (income), net. Non‑marketable equities measured using the measurement alternative (cost less impairment plus adjustments for observable price changes in orderly transactions for identical/similar investments), with changes recognized in other expense (income), net. Valuation of non‑marketable investments involves significant judgment, unobservable inputs, limited liquidity, and updates only upon observable transactions or impairment indicators.

title: Concentration of Credit Risk
heading: 1.9.1.12 Concentration of Credit Risk
start_phrase:
For the years ended December 31, 2020, 2019 
and 2018, the Company had no customer that accounted for greater than 10% of total net revenue.
summary:
- Restricted cash: Held primarily as collateral for multi-year lease agreements; $13.5 million at December 31, 2020 and $12.7 million at December 31, 2019; classified as non-current due to lease terms extending beyond one year; a portion expected to become unrestricted within the next year.
- Concentration of credit risk: No single customer accounted for more than 10% of net revenue in 2018–2020. Settlements receivable were concentrated among third-party processors—2020: approximately 59% and 27% with two processors; 2019: approximately 48%, 29%, and 9% with three parties; others insignificant.
- Financial instruments and risk mitigation: Exposures relate to cash and cash equivalents, restricted cash, marketable debt securities, settlements receivable, customer funds, and loans held for sale. Risks are mitigated by using creditworthy banks (though balances may exceed FDIC limits), holding a diversified portfolio of highly rated marketable debt securities, rapid settlement cycles (1–2 business days) for receivables, credit evaluations and ongoing monitoring for loans held for sale, and low risk on PPP loans due to government guarantees.
- Marketable debt securities: Portfolio includes U.S. government and agency securities, corporate bonds, commercial paper, municipal, and foreign government securities; all highly rated. Classified as available-for-sale and carried at fair value with unrealized gains/losses (net of taxes) recorded in stockholders’ equity. The company has the ability and intent to hold securities with unrealized losses long enough to recover amortized cost, potentially to maturity. Realized gains/losses are recognized in other expense (income), net, using specific identification.
- Equity securities: Includes marketable and non-marketable investments without control or significant influence. Marketable equity investments are measured at quoted market prices with changes recorded in other expense (income), net. Non-marketable equity investments use the measurement alternative (cost, less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for identical or similar investments of the same issuer), with adjustments recorded in other expense (income), net. Valuations rely on significant unobservable inputs due to illiquidity and inactive markets; carrying values are not adjusted absent observable transactions or impairment indicators, and require substantial management judgment.

Investments in equity securities
The
 Company holds marketable and non-marketable equity investments, over which the Company does not have a controlling interest or significantinfluence.
 Marketable equity investments are measured using quoted prices in active markets with changes recorded in other expense (income), net on theconsolidated
 statements of operations. Non-marketable equity investments have no readily determinable fair values and are measured using the measurementalternative,
 which is defined as cost, less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes from orderly transactions for identical or similar investments of thesame issuer. Adjustments ar
e recorded in other expense (income), net on the consolidated statements of operations.Non-marketable equity investments are valued using significant un
observable inputs or data in an inactive market and the valuation requires our judgmentdue
 to the absence of market prices and inherent lack of liquidity. The carrying value for these investments is not adjusted if there are no observable transactionsfor
 identical or similar investments of the same issuer or if there are no identified events or changes in circumstances that may indicate impairment. Valuations ofnon-marketable
 equity investments are inherently complex due to the lack of readily available market data. In addition, the determination of whether an orderlytransaction is for an ide
ntical or similar investment requires significant management95
judgment, including understanding the differences in the rights and obligations of the investments and the extent to which those differences would affect the fairvalues of those investments.
The
 Company  assesses  the  impairment  of  its  non-marketable  equity  investments  on  a  quarterly  basis.  The  impairment  analysis  encompasses  anassessment of
 the severity and duration of the impairment and a qualitative and quantitative analysis of other key factors including the investee’s financial metrics,market acceptanc
e of the investee’s product or technology, other competitive products or technology in the market, general market conditions, and the rate at whichthe
 investee is using its cash. If the investment is considered to be impaired, the Company will record an impairment in other income (expense), net on theconsolidated statemen

title: Fair Value of Financial Instruments
heading: 1.9.1.16 Fair Value of Financial Instruments
start_phrase:
The
 Company applies fair value accounting for all financial assets and liabilities that are recognized or disclosed at fair value in the financial statementson
 a recurring basis.
summary:
- Valuation and judgment for non-marketable equity investments, including assessing differing rights/obligations and their impact on fair value.
- Quarterly impairment assessment of non-marketable equity investments using qualitative and quantitative factors (severity/duration, investee financial metrics, product/technology acceptance, competitive landscape, market conditions, cash burn), with impairments recognized in other income (expense), net, and a new carrying value established.
- Customer funds definition (stored balances and cash-in-transit) and investment of a portion in short-term marketable debt securities; classification determined at purchase and reassessed each balance sheet date; designated as available-for-sale.
- Fair value measurement policy applied on a recurring basis with emphasis on market participant assumptions and maximizing observable inputs; disclosure within a three-level hierarchy:
  - Level 1: quoted prices in active markets for identical items.
  - Level 2: other observable inputs, direct or indirect, for substantially the full term.
  - Level 3: unobservable inputs when markets are inactive.
- Loans held for sale: classified upon purchase from an industrial bank partner with intent to sell to third-party investors; measured at the lower of amortized cost or fair value on an individual loan basis using discounted cash flow models.
- Valuation of loans incorporates market data, the effects of COVID-19 and historical recessionary periods; PPP loans reflect government guarantees and forgiveness in projected cash flows.
- Recognition of charges to transaction and loan losses when amortized cost exceeds fair value, with limited reversals only up to the point where amortized cost does not exceed fair value.
text:
Fair Value of Financial Instruments
The
 Company applies fair value accounting for all financial assets and liabilities that are recognized or disclosed at fair value in the financial statementson
 a recurring basis. Fair value accounting establishes a three-level hierarchy priority for disclosure of assets and liabilities recorded at fair value. The ordering ofpriority reflects
 the degree to which objective prices in external active markets are available to measure fair value. The classification of assets and liabilities withinthe hierarchy is based on wheth
er the inputs to the valuation methodology used for measurement are observable or unobservable.The Company utilizes valuat
ion techniques that maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs to the extent possible.The
 Company determines fair value based on assumptions that market participants would use in pricing an asset or liability in the principal or most advantageousmarket.
 When considering market participant assumptions in fair value measurements, the following fair value hierarchy distinguishes between observable andunobservable inputs, which are c
ategorized in one of the following levels:•
Level 1 Inputs: Unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities accessible to the reporting entity at the measurement date.•
Level 2 Inputs: Other than quoted prices included in Level 1 Inputs that are observable for the asset or liability, either directly or indirectly, forsubstantially the full term 
of the asset or liability.•
Level 3 Inputs: Unobservable inputs for the asset or liability used to measure fair value to the extent that observable inputs are not available, therebyallowing for situation
s in which there is little, if any, market activity for the asset or liability at measurement date.

title: Loans Held for Sale
heading: 1.9.1.17 Loans Held for Sale
start_phrase:
The Company classifies custom
 er loans as held for sale upon purchase from an industrial bank partner, as there is an available market for such loans and itis
 the Company’s intent to sell all of its rights, title, and interest in these loans to third-party investors.
summary:
- Valuation and impairment of non-marketable equity investments: quarterly assessments using judgment; factors include severity/duration of declines, investee financial metrics, product/technology acceptance, competition, market conditions, and cash burn; impairments recorded in other income (expense), net, with new carrying values established.
- Customer funds: stored balances/cash-in-transit; a portion invested in short-term marketable debt securities classified as available-for-sale and reviewed each reporting date.
- Fair value of financial instruments: application of fair value accounting on a recurring basis with emphasis on observable inputs and market participant assumptions; use of a three-level hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 other observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs).
- Loans held for sale: classified upon purchase from an industrial bank partner with intent to sell to third-party investors; measured at lower of amortized cost or fair value per loan using discounted cash flow models; estimates consider COVID-19 impacts, recessionary conditions, and PPP guarantees/forgiveness; losses recorded in transaction and loan losses with limited reversals; no reclassifications to held for investment to date.
- Settlements receivable: amounts due from payment processors, typically collected within 1–2 business days; no valuation allowance due to counterparties’ credit quality.
- Inventory: hardware and peripherals recorded at FIFO and lower of cost or net realizable value; write-downs for obsolescence/excess; stored at third-party warehouses and contract manufacturers.
- Deferred revenue: primarily upfront payments for website hosting and domain registrations; also includes unearned revenue for managed payments services tied to hardware sales.
- Investments in bitcoin: accounted for as an indefinite-lived intangible asset; tested continually for impairment with charges when fair value drops below carrying amount; no reversal of impairments before sale; $50 million acquired in Q4 2020 with no 2020 impairment.
- Property and equipment: cost less straight-line depreciation; useful lives—capitalized software 18 months, computer/data center equipment 2–3 years, furniture/fixtures 7 years, leasehold improvements lesser of 10 years or remaining lease term; gains/losses on disposals recorded in operating expenses.

text:
Loans Held for Sale
The Company classifies custom
er loans as held for sale upon purchase from an industrial bank partner, as there is an available market for such loans and itis
 the Company’s intent to sell all of its rights, title, and interest in these loans to third-party investors. Loans held for sale are recorded at the lower of amortizedcost
 or fair value determined on an individual loan basis. To determine the fair value the Company utilizes industry-standard valuation modeling, such asdiscounted

 of bitcoin becomes its new accounting basis. A subsequent reversal of a previously recognized impairment loss is prohibited until the sale of the asset. Inthe

title: Leases
heading: 1.9.1.24 Leases
start_phrase:
The Company leases office spa
ce and equipment under non-cancellable finance and operating leases with various expiration dates.
summary:
- Policy for internally developed software: costs are expensed until capitalization criteria are met; thereafter, costs are capitalized to property and equipment and amortized on a straight-line basis over the software’s useful life, with amortization recorded in product development costs. Amounts capitalized were $42.0 million (2020) and $22.5 million (2019); amortization expense was $19.8 million (2020), $18.9 million (2019), and $10.6 million (2018).
- Lease accounting under ASC 842 (adopted January 1, 2019): applied the optional transition method; elected practical expedients (no reassessment of existing/expired contracts, classifications, or initial direct costs) and the short-term lease exemption.
- Recognition and measurement: operating right-of-use (ROU) assets and lease liabilities measured at the present value of future lease payments using the Company’s incremental borrowing rate; ROU assets include prepaid amounts and incentives. Non-lease components (e.g., maintenance, utilities) are combined with lease payments and included as a single lease component. Amortization of ROU assets and accretion of lease liabilities are recorded as rent expense; finance lease accounting largely unchanged.
- Transition impacts: upon adoption, recognized $112.0 million of operating ROU assets and $135.6 million of operating lease liabilities; derecognized $149.0 million related to a build-to-suit asset and liability because the Company was no longer deemed the owner under ASC 842.
- Leasehold improvements: assessed for accounting “ownership.” If owner, capitalize and depreciate over the lesser of lease term or useful life; lessor allowances reduce the lease liability and ROU asset. If not owner, improvement payments are treated as lease payments.
- Asset retirement obligations (AROs) associated with leases: record at estimated fair value with an offsetting asset, using assumptions about legal obligations, timing, amounts, and discount/inflation rates; liabilities are accreted and assets depreciated. As of December 31, 2020, ARO liability was $3.7 million (gross of accretion) with a related asset of $1.1 million (net of depreciation).
- Scope of leases: office space and equipment under non-cancellable finance and operating leases with various expiration dates.

Leases
The Company leases office spa
ce and equipment under non-cancellable finance and operating leases with various expiration dates.The
 Company adopted Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 842, Leases (ASC 842) on January 1, 2019, and elected the optional transition methodto apply the transition provisions from the effective date of adoption
, which requires the Company to report the cumulative effect of the adoption of the standard onthe
 date of adoption with no changes to the prior period balances. Pursuant to the practical expedients, the Company elected not to reassess: (i) whether expired orexisting
 contracts are or contain leases, (ii) the lease classification for any expired or existing leases, or, (iii) initial direct costs for any existing leases. TheCompany
 elected to apply the short-term lease measurement and recognition exemption to its leases where applicable. Operating lease right-of-use assets andoperating
 lease liabilities are recognized at the present value of the future lease payments, generally for the base noncancellable lease term, at the leasecommencement date
 for each lease. The interest rate used to determine the present value of the future lease payments is the Company's incremental borrowing ratebecause
 the interest rate implicit in most of the Company's leases is not readily determinable. The Company's incremental borrowing rate is estimated toapproximate
 the interest rate that the Company would pay to borrow on a collateralized basis with similar terms and payments as the lease, and in economicenvironments
 where the leased asset is located. Operating lease right-of-use assets also include any prepaid lease payments and lease incentives. The Company'slease
 agreements generally contain lease and non-lease components. Non-lease components, which primarily include payments for maintenance and utilities, arecombined
 with lease payments and accounted for as a single lease component. The Company includes the fixed non-lease components in the determination of theright-of-use assets
 and operating lease liabilities. The Company records the amortization of the right of use asset and the accretion of lease liability as a componentof rent expense in the consol
idated statement of operations. The accounting for finance leases remained substantially unchanged.Upon adoption of ASC 842, the
 Company recognized $112.0 million of operating right-of-use lease assets and $135.6 million of operating lease liabilitieson

title: Business Combinations
heading: 1.9.1.25 Business Combinations
start_phrase:
The
 purchase price of an acquisition is allocated to the tangible and intangible assets acquired and liabilities assumed based on their estimated fair valuesat
 the acquisition dates.
summary:
- Business combinations: Purchase price allocated to identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value; excess recorded as goodwill. Measurement period up to one year allows adjustments to provisional amounts with offsets to goodwill; after the period, changes flow through the income statement.
- Long-lived assets impairment: Tested when indicators arise using undiscounted cash flows for recoverability; impairments measured to fair value via DCF, market data, or appraisals. No impairment charges recorded in the periods presented.
- Goodwill impairment: Annual test on December 31 and interim if needed; option for a qualitative “more-likely-than-not” assessment before quantitative testing. As of June 30, 2020, two reporting units (Seller and Cash App). No goodwill impairments recorded in the periods presented.
- Acquired intangibles: Comprised of acquired technology and customer relationships. Amortized straight-line over useful lives—technology in cost of revenue; customer relationships in operating expenses. Useful lives reassessed periodically.
- Customers payable: Amounts owed to sellers or Cash App customers net of Company revenue, including settlement timing differences (typically within one business day), amounts held per risk policies, amounts for customers without linked bank accounts, and liabilities for Cash App customer funds on deposit.
- Accrued transaction losses: Reserves for chargebacks and credit losses when collection from sellers is not possible (e.g., insolvency, disputes, fraud) and for certain Cash App activities (P2P via credit card, Cash for Business, Cash Card). Estimated using historical experience adjusted for new information, reasonable and supportable forecasts, and relevant market data (including COVID-19 impacts). Additions recorded in current operating results; realized losses are applied against the reserve.

The
 purchase price of an acquisition is allocated to the tangible and intangible assets acquired and liabilities assumed based on their estimated fair valuesat

rst, any subsequent adjustments would be recorded on the consolidated statements of operations.

title: Long-Lived Assets, including Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
heading: 1.9.1.26 Long-Lived Assets, including Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
start_phrase:
The
 Company evaluates the recoverability of property and equipment and finite lived intangible assets for impairment whenever events or circumstancesindicate
 that the carrying amounts of such assets may not be recoverable.
summary:
- Business combinations: Purchase price allocation to tangible and intangible assets and assumed liabilities at fair value; excess recorded as goodwill. During a measurement period of up to one year, adjustments to acquired assets/liabilities are offset to goodwill; after the period, changes flow through the income statement.
- Long-lived assets impairment: Property, equipment, and finite-lived intangibles are tested for impairment when indicators arise. Recoverability is assessed via undiscounted cash flows; if not recoverable, impairment is measured to fair value using methods such as discounted cash flows, market quotes, or independent appraisals. No impairment charges recorded in the periods presented.
- Goodwill impairment: Tested annually on December 31 and as needed upon triggering events. As of June 30, 2020, reporting segments are Seller and Cash App, aligning with CODM review. A qualitative “more-likely-than-not” screen may precede quantitative testing. No goodwill impairments recorded in the periods presented.
- Acquired intangibles: Include acquired technology and customer relationships. Amortized on a straight-line basis—technology within cost of revenue, customer relationships within operating expenses. Useful lives are reassessed periodically for potential revision.
- Customers payable: Represents amounts due to sellers or Cash App customers net of revenue earned, including settlement timing differences (typically settled within one business day), amounts held under risk management policies, amounts for customers without linked bank accounts, and liabilities for Cash App customer funds on deposit.
- Accrued transaction losses: Exposure to chargebacks and losses from Cash App activities (peer-to-peer payments from credit cards, Cash for Business, Cash Card). Loss estimates are based on historical experience adjusted for new information and reasonable, supportable forecasts, incorporating relevant market data and COVID-19/recessionary conditions. Additions are recognized in current operations; realized losses are offset against the reserve.
text:
The
 Company evaluates the recoverability of property and equipment and finite lived intangible assets for impairment whenever events or circumstancesindicate

nized to the extent that the carrying amount exceeds its fair value. Fair value is determined through variousvaluation
 techniques including discounted cash flow models, quoted market values, and third–party independent appraisals, as considered necessary. For theperiods presented, the Company had 
recorded no impairment charges.The
 Company performs a goodwill impairment test annually on December 31 and more frequently if events and circumstances indicate that the assetmight
 be impaired. An impairment loss is recognized to the extent that the carrying amount exceeds the reporting unit’s fair value. Effective June 30, 2020, theCompany

 and determine whether further action is needed. If, after assessing the totality of events or circumstances, the Company determines it is not more likelythan
 not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying amount, then performing the two-step impairment test is unnecessary. For the periodspresented, the Company had reco
rded no impairment charges.Acquired
 intangibles consist of acquired technology and customer relationships associated with various acquisitions. Acquired technology is amortizedover
 its estimated useful life on a straight-line basis within cost of revenue. Customer relationships acquired are amortized on a straight-line basis over theirestimated useful lives within operating expenses. The C
ompany evaluates the remaining estimated useful life of its intangible assets being amortized on an ongoingbasis to determine whethe
r events and circumstances warrant a revision to the remaining period of amortization.

title: Accrued Transaction Losses
heading: 1.9.1.28 Accrued Transaction Losses
start_phrase:
The
 Company is exposed to potential credit losses related to transactions processed by sellers that are subsequently subject to chargebacks when theCompany
 is unable to collect from the sellers primarily due to insolvency, disputes between a seller and their customer, or due to fraudulent transactions.
summary:
- Business combinations: Purchase price is allocated to acquired assets and assumed liabilities at fair value; excess is recorded as goodwill. During a measurement period of up to one year, adjustments to provisional amounts are recorded with an offset to goodwill; after the period ends, any changes flow through the income statement.
- Long-lived assets: Property, equipment, and finite-lived intangibles are tested for recoverability when indicators arise, using undiscounted cash flows; impairments are measured to fair value via DCFs, market quotes, or appraisals. No impairment charges were recorded for the periods presented.
- Goodwill: Tested annually on December 31, or more frequently if needed. The company may first perform a qualitative assessment to determine if a quantitative test is necessary. Following a June 30, 2020 reorganization, reporting units align with two segments: Seller and Cash App. No goodwill impairments were recorded for the periods presented.
- Acquired intangibles: Include acquired technology and customer relationships. Amortized straight-line over estimated useful lives—technology within cost of revenue; customer relationships within operating expenses. Useful lives are reassessed on an ongoing basis.
- Customers payable: Represents amounts owed to sellers or Cash App customers (net of company revenue), including timing differences (typically settled within one business day), funds held per risk policies, amounts for customers without linked bank accounts, and Cash App customer funds on deposit.
- Accrued transaction losses: Reflect potential credit losses from chargebacks and certain Cash App activities (P2P via credit card, Cash for Business, Cash Card). Loss rates are estimated from historical experience adjusted for new information and reasonable, supportable forecasts (including COVID-19 impacts) and relevant market data. Additions are recorded in current operations; realized losses offset the reserve. Classified in transaction and loan losses, except free P2P losses, which are in sales and marketing.
- Segments: Effective June 30, 2020, two reportable segments—Seller (payments, software, hardware, and financial services for sellers) and Cash App (P2P payments, Cash Card, bitcoin, and stock investing for individuals).
- Recently adopted accounting standards: ASU 2020-06 on convertible instruments will be early adopted January 1, 2021 using a modified retrospective approach. Expected effects: retained earnings reduced by $103.5 million; other paid-in capital reduced by $502.7 million; convertible notes increased by $399.2 million; no expected impact on statements of operations or cash flows; EPS uses the if-converted method.
- Recently issued standards not yet adopted: ASU 2020-10 (Codification Improvements) effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2020, including interims; not expected to have a material impact.

title: Recently adopted accounting pronouncements
heading: 1.9.1.30.1 Recently adopted accounting pronouncements
start_phrase:
In August 2020, the Financial Accounting Standards Boar
d (FASB) issued Accounting Standards Update (ASU) No. 2020-06, Accounting for Convertible Instruments and Contracts in an Entity's Own Equity
, as part of its overall simplification initiative to reduce costs and complexity of applying accounting standardswhile maintaining or improving the usefulness of the information provided to users of financial statements.
summary:
- Classification of certain reserves: amounts related to transaction and loan losses are recorded in transaction and loan losses on the income statement, except costs tied to the free peer-to-peer Cash App service, which are recorded in sales and marketing.
- Segment reporting change (effective June 30, 2020): the company now reports two segments—Seller (managed payments, software, hardware, and financial services for sellers) and Cash App (consumer financial tools including P2P payments, Cash Card, bitcoin, and stock investing).
- Recently adopted accounting guidance (ASU 2020-06): early adoption planned for January 1, 2021 using a modified retrospective approach; eliminates most separations of convertible debt into debt and equity, requires if-converted method for EPS (already in use); expected impacts include a $103.5 million reduction to retained earnings, a $502.7 million reduction to additional paid-in capital, and a $399.2 million increase to convertible notes; no expected effect on the statements of operations or cash flows.
- Recently issued but not yet adopted guidance (ASU 2020-10): Codification improvements effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2020; includes clarifications such as income tax presentation related to other comprehensive income; not expected to have a material impact; evaluation ongoing.
text:
In August 2020, the Financial Accounting Standards Boar
d (FASB) issued Accounting Standards Update (ASU) No. 2020-06, Accounting for Convertible Instruments and Contracts in an Entity's Own Equity
, as part of its overall simplification initiative to  reduce costs and complexity of applying accounting standardswhile maintaining
 or improving the usefulness of the information provided to users of financial statements. Among other changes, the new guidance removes fromGAAP
 separation models for convertible debt that require the convertible debt to be separated into a debt and equity component, unless the conversion feature isrequired
 to be bifurcated and accounted for as a derivative or the debt is issued at a substantial premium. As a result, after adopting the guidance, entities will nolonger
 separately present such embedded conversion features in equity, and will instead account for the convertible debt wholly as debt. The new guidance alsorequires
 use of the "if-converted" method when calculating the dilutive impact of convertible debt on earnings per share, which is consistent with the Company’scurrent
 accounting treatment under the current guidance. The guidance is effective for financial statements issued for fiscal years beginning after December 15,2021,
 and interim periods within those fiscal years, with early adoption permitted, but only at the beginning of the fiscal year. The Company plans to early adoptthe
 new guidance on January 1, 2021 using the modified retrospective approach and expects to record a cumulative effect of adoption of $103.5 million reductionto
 retained earnings. The Company expects the impact of adoption to result in a reduction to other paid in capital of $502.7 million related to amounts attributableto
 conversion options that had previously been recorded in equity. Additionally, the Company also expects to record an increase to its convertible notes balance byan
 aggregate amount of $399.2 million as a result of reversal of the separation of the convertible debt between debt and equity. There is no expected impact to theCompany’s statements of oper
ations or cash flows as the result of the adoption of this ASU.

heading: 1.9.7.2 Weebly, Inc.
start_phrase:
On
 May 31, 2018, the Company acquired 100% of the outstanding shares of Weebly, a technology company that offers customers website hosting anddomain
 name registration solutions.
summary:
- Note 7 summarizes acquisitions. The Company completed other, non-material acquisitions totaling $126.7 million (2020), $25.2 million (2019), and $15.4 million (2018), resulting in additional intangible assets and goodwill; pro forma financial information was not presented. Goodwill and acquired intangibles from these deals are not expected to be tax-deductible.

- Weebly, Inc. acquisition (May 31, 2018):
  - Strategic rationale: integrate Weebly’s website hosting and domain solutions with the Company’s in-person and online offerings to support omnichannel sellers, expand the global customer base, and add recurring revenue.
  - Consideration: $132.4 million in cash plus 2,418,271 Class A shares valued at $140.1 million, totaling $272.5 million. An additional $17.7 million was paid to settle employee options; $2.6 million of this was recorded as post-combination compensation (excluded from purchase consideration). Third-party transaction costs were insignificant. Weebly’s results have been consolidated since closing.
  - Accounting: Business combination with assets and liabilities recorded at fair value; excess recorded as goodwill (not amortized, subject to annual impairment testing).
  - Purchase price allocation (in thousands): current assets $46,978 (including $25,758 cash); intangible customer assets $42,700; technology $14,900; trade name $11,300; other intangibles $961; total liabilities assumed $(37,509) including deferred revenue of $22,800; identifiable net assets $79,330; goodwill $193,209; total $272,539.
  - Measurement period adjustments (2019): increases to goodwill $3.7 million, current assets $2.3 million, and tax liabilities $4.7 million; no impact to the statements of operations.
  - Holdback: As of December 31, 2020, $0.5 million in cash and 8,873 shares remained withheld for indemnification and certain tax exposures.
  - Tax: Goodwill and acquired intangibles are not expected to be tax-deductible. Deferred tax assets (from NOLs and R&D credits) and deferred tax liabilities (from intangibles and deferred revenue) arose; a valuation allowance was recorded against the net acquired deferred tax asset due to realizability uncertainties.
  - Impact: The acquisition did not have a material effect on reported revenue or net loss in presented periods.

 May 2023. On May 28, 2020, the Company amended the credit agreement for the 2020 Credit Facility to permit the Company’s wholly owned subsidiary,Square
 Capital, LLC (“Square Capital”), to incur indebtedness in an aggregate principal amount of up to $500.0 million pursuant to the Paycheck ProtectionProgram
 Liquidity Facility (“PPPLF) authorized under the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. In connection with its convertible debt offerings in November 2020, theCompany entered into a second a

Loans
 under the 2020 Credit Facility bear interest, at the Company’s option of (i) a base rate based on the highest of the prime rate, the federal funds rateplus

ion remained available for draw. The Company incurred $0.7 million and $0.6 million in unused commitment fees for theyears

- Conversion features: Initial conversion rate is 8.2641 shares per $1,000 principal (≈$121.01 per share). - Accounting: The notes were bifurcated into liability and equity components. The liability component was measured at the fair value of comparable non-convertible debt; the equity component (conversion option) was $154.6 million and is not remeasured while equity classification is maintained. start_phrase: In connection with the offering of the 2027 Notes, the Company entered into convertible note hedge transactions (2027 convertible note hedges) withcertain financial institution counterparties (2027 Notes Counterparties) whereby the Company has the option to purchase a total of approximately 1.92 millionshares of its Class A common stock at a price of approximately $299.13 per share.
summary:
- Discloses effective interest rates of the liability components for the company’s convertible notes: 2027 (3.66%), 2026 (3.35%), 2025 (3.81%), 2023 (4.69%), and 2022 (5.34%).
- Details convertible note hedge and warrant transactions associated with each note issuance (2027, 2026, 2025, 2023, 2022), including:
  - Size of share coverage under hedges and warrants.
  - Strike prices for hedges (aligned with initial conversion prices) and higher strike prices for warrants.
  - Cash outlay for purchasing hedges and cash proceeds from selling warrants.
  - Purpose: reduce dilution upon conversion and/or offset cash payments above principal; effectively increase the conversion price via the paired hedge/warrant structures.
- Explains accounting treatment: instruments are indexed to the company’s own stock, equity-classified, recorded in stockholders’ equity, not accounted for as derivatives, not remeasured each period; net costs recorded as a reduction to additional paid-in capital.
- Notes activity on the 2022 instruments: partial exercise of the 2022 convertible note hedges to offset share settlement of converted 2022 Notes; hedges net share settled; 9.4 million shares received cumulatively by December 31, 2020 (including 2.2 million in 2020).
- Introduces Note 14 – Income Taxes: presents the domestic and foreign components of income (loss) before income taxes for 2020, 2019, and 2018, showing positive consolidated pre-tax income in 2020 and 2019 and a loss in 2018.

start_phrase: The domestic and foreign components of income (loss) before income taxes are as follows (in thousands):
summary:
- Convertible note hedge and warrant transactions
  - 2023 Notes: Purchased convertible note hedges covering 11.1 million shares at a strike of approximately $77.85 per share for $172.6 million; sold 2023 warrants to the 2018 Counterparties for 11.1 million shares at approximately $109.26 per share, receiving $112.1 million. Combined, these are intended to reduce dilution and/or offset cash paid above principal on conversion and effectively raise the conversion price from ~$77.85 to ~$109.26 per share.
  - 2022 Notes: Purchased convertible note hedges covering ~19.2 million shares at ~$22.95 per share for $92.1 million; sold 2022 warrants to the 2017 Counterparties for ~19.2 million shares at ~$31.18 per share, receiving $57.2 million. Combined, these are intended to reduce dilution/offset cash and effectively raise the conversion price from ~$22.95 to ~$31.18 per share. A pro-rata portion of the 2022 hedges was exercised (net share settled); by December 31, 2020 the Company had received 9.4 million shares (2.2 million in 2020).
  - Accounting: Instruments are indexed to the Company’s own stock, equity-classified, recorded in stockholders’ equity, not accounted for as derivatives, and not remeasured each period. Net costs recorded as a reduction to additional paid-in capital.

- Income taxes (Note 14)
  - Income (loss) before income taxes (in thousands): 2020: $215,967 (Domestic $369,016; Foreign $(153,049)); 2019: $378,213 (Domestic $456,335; Foreign $(78,122)); 2018: $(36,127) (Domestic $44,538; Foreign $(80,665)).

  - Effective tax rate reconciliation shows low effective rates (2020: 1.3%; 2019: 0.7%; 2018: (6.4)%) driven by credits, valuation allowance changes, share-based compensation, foreign rate differences, and other non-deductible items.
  - Deferred taxes (in thousands): 2020 gross deferred tax assets $1,337,089 offset by valuation allowance $(1,238,010), net DTA $99,079; deferred tax liabilities $(91,301); net deferred tax asset $7,778. Significant DTAs include NOLs, tax credit carryforwards, accrued expenses, share-based compensation; valuation allowance maintained due to loss history in certain jurisdictions and increased by ~$378.4 million (2020) and ~$140.5 million (2019).
  - Carryforwards: As of 12/31/2020, federal NOLs $3,472.5 million (begin to expire 2031), state NOLs $3,888.9 million (begin to expire 2021), foreign NOLs $500.2 million (no expiration). Credits: federal $196.8 million (begin to expire 2029), state $123.3 million (no expiration), Canadian $2.7 million (begin to expire 2037), Australian $4.2 million (no expiration), and California Enterprise Zone credits $3.4 million (begin to expire 2023). Potential Section 382/383 limitations noted but not expected to materially reduce utilization.
  - Unrecognized tax benefits: $295.2 million at 12/31/2020; $13.2 million would affect the annual ETR if recognized; remainder would adjust the valuation allowance. Interest and penalties accrued of $1.4 million (2020). Possible decrease in unrecognized tax benefits up to $11.4 million over next 12 months.
  - Tax audits and positions: Under examination in California (2013–2014) and Texas (2015–2017); various tax years from 2009–2019 remain open. Certain non-U.S. subsidiary earnings ($1.4 million at 12/31/2020) are permanently reinvested; no deferred U.S. tax provided.

- Stockholders’ equity (Note 15)
  - Preferred stock: Authorized 100,000,000 shares (par $0.0000001); none outstanding at 12/31/2020.
  - Common stock: Dual-class structure. Class A: one vote per share. Class B: ten votes per share; generally converts to Class A upon transfer. No preemptive or subscription rights; no redemption or sinking fund provisions. No dividends declared in 2020.
  - Authorized shares: 1,000,000,000 Class A; 500,000,000 Class B (par $0.0000001).
  - Outstanding at 12/31/2020: 390,187,079 Class A; 65,997,697 Class B.
  - Note references to options and awards granted after the November 2015 IPO (section cut off).

Employee Stock Purchase Plan
On
 November 17, 2015, the Company’s 2015 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) became effective. The ESPP allows eligible employees to purchaseshares
 of the Company’s common stock at a discount through payroll deductions of up to 15% of their eligible compensation, (or 25% for offering periods thatcommence
 after November 1, 2019), subject to any plan limitations. The ESPP provides for 12-month offering periods. The offering periods are scheduled to starton the first
 trading day on or after May 15 and November 15 of each year. Each offering period includes two purchase periods, which begin on the first trading dayon
 or after November 15 and May 15, and ending on the last trading day on or before May 15 and November 15, respectively.  Employees are able to purchaseshares
 at 85% of the lower of the fair market value of the Company’s common stock on the first trading day of the offering period or the last trading day of thepurchase
 period. The number of shares available for sale under the ESPP will be increased annually on the first day of each fiscal year, equal to the least of (i)8,400,000
 shares, (ii) 1% of the outstanding shares of the Company’s common stock as of the last day of the immediately preceding fiscal year, or (iii) such otheramount
 as determined by the administrator. As of December 31, 2020, 5,829,106 shares had been purchased under the ESPP and 17,816,248 shares were availablefor future issuance under 
the ESPP.

title: Litigation
heading: 1.9.18.2 Litigation
start_phrase: The Company is currently subject to, and may in the future be involved in, various litigation matters, legal claims, and investigations.
summary:
- Summary of operating lease commitments: As of December 31, 2020, undiscounted future minimum lease payments under non-cancelable operating leases total $566.3 million, with significant amounts due thereafter ($240.8 million). After adjustments for interest ($82.8 million), leases executed but not yet commenced ($21.9 million), and lease incentives/held-for-sale transfers ($19.2 million), the total is $442.4 million. Operating lease rental expense recognized was $75.2 million (2020), $32.5 million (2019), and $23.3 million (2018).
- Litigation: The company is involved in ordinary-course legal matters and investigations. While outcomes are uncertain and could be material to results in a particular period, the company does not currently expect a material adverse effect on overall financial position, liquidity, or results of operations.
- Tax contingencies: The Texas Comptroller completed a sales and use tax audit for 1/1/2015–4/30/2018 and plans to assess $38 million (including interest and penalties), asserting certain services are taxable. The company disputes this; however, if unsuccessful, it could owe additional taxes, penalties, and interest for the audited and subsequent periods, potentially materially. The company is also subject to examinations by multiple tax authorities, regularly assesses exposure, believes current tax provisions are adequate, and may adjust provisions if outcomes differ from expectations.

start_phrase: Effective June 30, 2020, the Company changed its operating segments to reflect the manner in which the Company's CODM reviews and assessesperformance.

Notes exclusion of the Caviar business (sold in 2019) and reconciles total segment revenue to consolidated net revenue (adding Caviar revenue of $145,913 in 2019 and $148,608 in 2018; total net revenue $9,497,578 in 2020, $4,713,500 in 2019, $3,298,177 in 2018). Reconciles total segment gross profit to income before income taxes by deducting product development, sales and marketing, general and administrative, transaction and loan losses, amortization of acquired customer assets, and interest expense, and reflecting a 2019 gain on sale of an asset group and other expense (income), yielding income (loss) before taxes of $215,967 (2020), $378,213 (2019), and $(36,127) (2018). States geographic revenue is based on seller/customer addresses, with a table to follow.

title: NOTE 21 - SUBSEQUENT EVENTS
heading: 1.9.21 NOTE 21 - SUBSEQUENT EVENTS
start_phrase: On January 28, 2021, the Company entered into a third amendment to the credit agreement for the 2020 Credit Facility to increase the amount ofindebtedness that Square Capital is permitted to incur pursuant to the PPPLF from an aggregate principal amount of up to $500 million to an aggregate principalamount of up to $1.0 billion.
summary:
- Subsequent events related to financing: On January 28, 2021, the Company amended its 2020 Credit Facility to raise Square Capital’s permitted PPPLF indebtedness limit from $500 million to $1.0 billion.
- PPPLF activity: On January 29, 2021, Square Capital submitted a PPPLF Letter of Agreement to the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco to obtain additional advances secured by second-round PPP loans. As of February 23, 2021, approximately $376.3 million of PPPLF advances were outstanding and fully collateralized by PPP loans.
- PPP participation: In February 2021, Square Capital began participating in the second round of the PPP, accepting applications from certain existing customers who previously received PPP loans through Square Capital. The process was expedited using prior application data; these loans are U.S. government–guaranteed and may be forgiven if criteria are met.

- Assurance level: Management notes controls provide reasonable, not absolute, assurance and involve cost-benefit judgments.

- Management’s ICFR assessment: Management is responsible for ICFR; assessed effectiveness using the COSO 2013 framework and concluded ICFR was effective as of December 31, 2020.

summary:
- Part IV, Item 15 outlines materials filed with the Form 10-K: (1) consolidated financial statements (referenced to Part II, Item 8), (2) financial statement schedules (omitted if inapplicable or included in the statements/notes), and (3) an Exhibit Index of documents filed or incorporated by reference pursuant to Item 601 of Regulation S-K.
- The Exhibit Index includes:
  - Corporate and governance documents: Agreement and Plan of Reorganization (Weebly acquisition), Amended and Restated Certificate of Incorporation, Amended and Restated Bylaws, and description of Class A common stock.
  - Securities and financing instruments: multiple indentures and forms of convertible senior notes (due 2022, 2023, 2025, 2026, 2027), stock certificate, investors’ rights agreement, convertible note hedge confirmations, and warrant confirmations.
  - Compensation and management contracts: indemnification agreements; 2015 Equity Incentive Plan; 2015 Employee Stock Purchase Plan; 2009 Stock Plan; Executive Incentive Compensation Plan; Outside Director Compensation Policy; change of control and severance agreements; and executive offer letters (including for Jack Dorsey, Alyssa Henry, and Amrita Ahuja).
  - Real estate and credit facilities: principal office lease at 1455 Market Street (and multiple amendments) and a revolving credit agreement with subsequent amendments.
  - Commercial and manufacturing arrangements: master development and supply agreements with TDK, Cheng Uei, and ON Semiconductor, including ASIC development and related amendment.
  - Government program arrangements: Paycheck Protection Program Liquidity Facility letters.
  - Corporate and compliance materials: list of subsidiaries; auditor consents (Ernst & Young LLP and KPMG LLP); CEO/CFO certifications under Sarbanes-Oxley Sections 302 and 906; and Inline XBRL exhibits (instance, schema, calculation, definition, labels, presentation) plus the cover page interactive data file.
- Footnotes clarify: items filed herewith (*); management or compensatory plans (+); exhibits with portions omitted under confidential treatment (#, Rule 406); and that the Section 906 certifications (†, Exhibit 32.1) are furnished, not filed or incorporated by reference.
- Item 16 states there is no Form 10-K summary.

summary:
- Signature and authorization: The 2020 Form 10-K of Square, Inc. is signed on February 23, 2021 by Jack Dorsey (President, CEO, and Chairman). A Power of Attorney authorizes Jack Dorsey, Amrita Ahuja, and Sivan Whiteley to sign amendments. The filing lists signatures, titles, and dates for the CEO, CFO, Chief Accounting Officer, and all directors.

- Outside Director Compensation Policy: Policy for non-employee directors, adopted November 4, 2015, effective November 18, 2015, last amended October 21, 2020, with amendments effective January 1, 2021.
  - Cash compensation: $40,000 annual retainer; additional annual retainers—Audit & Risk Chair $20,000; Compensation Chair $15,000; Nominating & Corporate Governance Chair $10,000; Capital Compliance & Governance Chair $15,000; committee members—Audit $10,000; Compensation $5,000; Nominating & Corporate Governance $2,500; Capital Compliance & Governance $5,000. Paid quarterly in arrears; no per-meeting fees; chairs do not also receive member fees for the same committee.
  - Equity compensation: Outside Directors may receive equity (excluding ISOs) under the 2015 Equity Incentive Plan.
    - Election to receive RSUs in lieu of cash retainers: Directors can convert quarterly cash retainers into fully vested RSUs based on the quarter-end share closing price; elections/revocations require written notice at least 10 business days before the Retainer Accrual Date and cannot be made during blackout periods; exceptions allowed to avoid legal or regulatory issues.
    - Automatic awards: Non-discretionary RSU grants—
      - Initial Award on joining the Board (other than on an Annual Meeting date): grant-date fair value of $250,000, prorated by months since the last Annual Meeting; vests on the earlier of one year or the next Annual Meeting, subject to service.
      - Annual Award at each Annual Meeting: $250,000 grant-date fair value; same vesting terms.
      - Lead Independent Director additional Annual Award: $70,000 grant-date fair value; same vesting terms.
      - Change in Control: all such awards fully vest.
  - Additional provisions: Plan terms apply unless inconsistent; the Board may revise, suspend, or terminate the policy at any time.

- Exhibit 21.1 (Major Subsidiaries): Lists key subsidiaries and jurisdictions, including Square Capital, LLC; Cash App Investing, LLC (Delaware, U.S.); Squareup International Ltd (Ireland); Squareup Pte. Ltd. (Singapore); Square Canada, Inc.; Square Technologies, Inc. (Canada); Squareup Europe Ltd; Squareup (UK) Ltd (United Kingdom); Decentralized Global Payments, S.L.U. (Spain); Verse Payments Lithuania UAB (Lithuania). Other subsidiaries omitted as not significant.

- Exhibit 23.1 (Auditor consents): Ernst & Young LLP consents to incorporation by reference of its February 23, 2021 reports on 2020 financial statements and internal control over financial reporting. KPMG LLP consents to incorporation by reference of its report on 2018 financial statements (dated February 27, 2019, except Note 19 as of February 23, 2021).

- Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2 (SOX 302 certifications): CEO (Jack Dorsey) and CFO (Amrita Ahuja) certify review of the 10-K, accuracy and fair presentation, design and evaluation of disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, disclosure of changes in ICFR, and disclosure of significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, and fraud to auditors and the audit committee.

- Exhibit 32.1 (SOX 906 certifications): CEO and CFO certify that the 10-K complies with Exchange Act reporting requirements and fairly presents, in all material respects, the company’s financial condition and results of operations (dated February 23, 2021).

Outside Director Compensation Policy(Adopted On November 4, 2015; Effective As Of November 18, 2015; As Last Amended on October 21, 2020)
Square,
 Inc. (the “Company” )  believes that the granting of cash compensation and equity to members of its Board of Directors(the 
“Board,” and members of the Board, the “Directors” )  represents an effective tool to attract, retain, and reward Directorswho are
 not employees of the Company (the “Outside Directors” ).  This Outside Director Compensation Policy (the “Policy” ) isintended
 to formalize the Company’s policy regarding grants of cash compensation and equity to its Outside Directors. Unlessdefined
 in this Policy, capitalized terms are defined in the Company’s 2015 Equity Incentive Plan, as may be amended from timeto
 time (the “Plan” ). Each Outside Director is solely responsible for any tax obligations he or she incurs from the receipt of anycompensation
 under this Policy. The Company will reimburse each Outside Director for reasonable, customary, and documentedtravel expenses in connection with attending meetings of the Board or any committee of the Board.
This Policy is amended effective as of January 1, 2021 (the 
“Effective Date” ). 1. CASH RETAINERS
Annual Cash Retainer
Each Outside Director will be paid an annual cash retainer of $40,000.
